understand:founder.summary: The founder is asking for short comic brand spots carried by a duo, like the Israeli duos they named, not a serial whose plot needs labels. On 15 Nov they said it: Timo and Luna as presenters and faces of the brand, in adventures and comic bits, "international, humorous and nice, at eye level". Every reference is a pair of opposite characters who bicker in everyday speech through one situation and one joke, with the brand as the answer. The latest film is the reverse: 44.8 seconds, 36 on-screen texts, six labels explaining a twist, the product as a feature card, an empty glossy 3D world. Next time start from a joke that is funny read aloud.
points: The founder's clearest statement of taste is 15 Nov 14:43: Timo and Luna as 'the presenters, the duo and the face' of the brand, in 'adventures, comic things', in the style of three Israeli campaigns, 'only ours international, humorous and nice, speaking at eye level', so that people 'appreciate us more'; season 2 episode 1 does not play or sound like that.

Every campaign they named is a comic duo: Bisli's Grill and Barbi (animated, created 1998, brought back February 2026), the car-insurance pigeons (two animated pigeons inside real footage, about 2012 to 2022), the Electric Company's Sheka and Teka (two fur puppets, since 2002) and Toto-Winner's Double and Pass (animated presenters, since 2013).

I could not verify any 'pigeons of the Electric Company': the pigeons belong to a direct insurer and the Electric Company's duo are the puppets, so my reading is that the founder merged two campaigns, and both fit the same class.

In the spot descriptions I could find, one spot is one everyday situation and one joke, and the brand resolves it or signs it with one fixed line: a bomb squad whose nerves Bisli 'defuses', an anxious pigeon calmed by a relaxed one who explains how easy the insurer is, a power fault that turns into ordering pizza, a closing rhyme for the lottery form.

These duos are remembered for voices and banter, not plots: each pair has opposite temperaments, is voiced by well-known comedians (Tal Friedman and Eli Finish for the pigeons, Tzion Baruch and Udi Gottschalk for Bisli in 2009 to 2013), and kept the same look for five to more than twenty years.

A trade report says Bisli's February 2026 comeback rebuilt its two characters with AI tools and paired them with a stand-up comedian, so the founder's reference is current, and its bar is the writing and the voices, not the tool.

International equivalents: M&M's Red and Yellow (cocky schemer and lovable dullard, from 1995), the Compare the Market meerkats Aleksandr and Sergei (from 2009), Apple's Mac and PC (66 aired spots) and Duolingo's owl on TikTok (its team says it never sells outright); they share a fixed character people know at once, one joke per film, the product inside the joke, and years of consistency.
The latest film runs 44.8 seconds with 12 clips, 14 captioned spoken lines and 36 separate on-screen text elements, one new text about every 1.2 seconds.
Six of those texts are narrator labels that explain the story (for example 'his plan for having no plan' and 'he planned her too'), which shows the joke does not land through picture and voice.

The plot leans on season 1 (why 'Done' is her word, the folder, the suitcase's name, the stare) and on a twist about planning not to plan, so a first-time viewer has nothing to laugh at, while a reference spot works as the first one you ever see.

The product appears as a brand card with a typed sentence and four ticks twice, then a four-line end card, about 13 of 45 seconds in all, which reads as a feature list, whereas in the references the product is the punchline.
The dialogue is tidy written English ('I packed one sentence', 'Step three: Luna carries the folder') with no interruption, slang or real reaction, which is the opposite of 'at eye level'.
Nothing a sports traveller recognises happens: no game, no crowd, no trip trouble, only a suitcase and a folder on an empty street, so it cannot feel 'authentic'.

The glossy vinyl-toy 3D figures, one sunset light, locked camera and empty streets are, in my judgment, what generic AI video looks like, and the founder asked on 16 and on 17 Nov that it not feel like AI.

The founder praised twice (14 Nov 'everything is great'; 15 Nov 13:35 'I liked it very much', most likely the 37-second 'The Bet') and both times rejected what followed within two days, so praise for one film did not approve the line that grew out of it.

Constant since 12 Nov: highest quality, no blunders, no wasted money; new on 17 Nov: show nothing until it is finished, after the notes show this one episode cost about 47 dollars (two takes of every shot plus nine reshoots) against about 34 for all four episodes of season 1.

understand:diagnosis.summary: The film fails at script and performance, not at rendering. A scroller leaves inside two seconds: a static wide shot, a man pointing at a blank sheet, two text blocks, a hook that needs season 1. Nothing is funny: eleven intended jokes, no surprise, and a reveal only a label can explain. It reads as AI and as an advert because of 141 on-screen words, six explaining labels, 12.8 seconds of brand graphics from second 3.8, characters alone in most shots and grinning after each line, machine voices no human heard, and a stock toy look. The cat, the suitcase, the palette, the push image and the clean render were fine.
points: First two seconds: the scroller swipes, because 0.0-3.7 s is one locked wide shot of a man pointing at a blank sheet with two text blocks already up ("he says he quit planning", "No notes. No folder. One sentence."), only four words are spoken by 1.7 s, and the hook is about notes that only a season 1 viewer ever saw.

It is not funny: the eleven intended jokes are claims, callbacks and explanations with no surprise; the best line ("Nine words. I counted.", 4.1-6.0 s) is buried under a typing product card, and the only physical gag (small Luna shoving the giant suitcase while Timo strolls, 11.9-14.7 s) is a 2.8-second transition spoiled by the label "so today, she pushes".

The reveal fails: the cat sits on top of the suitcase beside Luna's face at 14.5-17.5 s, Timo says "Maybe... the cat?", and one cut later (21.5 s) the cat is inside on a plain untitled blue book, so only the label "his plan for having no plan" tells you what you are looking at, and one slim folder does not explain a suitcase too heavy to push.

The pay-off shrinks instead of growing: "Step two: Luna pushes Big Yellow?!" is followed by the smaller "Step three: Luna carries the folder." and a scoreboard label ("his plan wins. she carries."), Luna obeys for no reason, Timo comes across as smug, and nobody gets a reaction shot at the reveal.

Six labels (15.8 of 44.8 s) do the storytelling because the picture cannot: the clip prompts say the phone screen "is never seen" and the folder's "pages are never seen", so the two things the plot is about exist only as overlays, and the labels answer the founder's 15 Nov "I did not understand the plot" by explaining instead of showing.

The text load is that of a subtitled explainer: 36 text elements and 141 words in 44.8 s (only 47 are spoken), text on screen for 40.4 s, up to seven elements at once (7.4-8.9 s) in four type styles, and being told what you just saw is a large part of why it feels dumb.

It reads as an advert from second 3.8: the brand plate arrives before any joke, brand graphics fill 12.8 s (29%), there are two feature cards with four ticks each plus synthetic typing, ding and pops, about 4.3 s of frozen frames are held under the tick cards and the end card, and a four-block end card with "season 2 · ep 1 · follow for ep 2" covers Timo's stare from 41.3 s, so the stare is never seen without text.

Acting and staging: nine of the ten dialogue prompts ask for a smile, grin or beam ("ends beaming", "like a presenter"), so Luna says the indignant "That's MY word!" grinning (9.0-11.5 s); seven of twelve shots (28.5 s) show one human alone facing the camera, no shot has two speakers (the script record says those shots were removed on purpose), and the two never touch and barely look at each other, although the founder asked for "interactions between the characters".

The look is the stock generated-3D look: smooth vinyl figures in the same pastel golden light indoors and out, a New York with no other people and no signs, the same row of houses behind both speakers, three eye designs for Timo in one film (half-lidded slits at 4-8 s, black dots at 30 s, white round eyes at 39-44 s), and movement that floats evenly out of a still start under a locked camera with slow digital push-ins.

Voices, judged from documents and measurement because I could not hear them: each was generated clip by clip from adjectives in the prompt, passed through a voice cleaner and never checked by a human ear (the posting kit says so), and my rough pitch estimate puts Timo near 107-121 Hz in two shots (4-6 s, 30-32 s) and 143-150 Hz in two others (12.6-14.1 s, 18-20 s), which suggests he does not sound like one person.

The lines are ad copy, not talk ("No notes. No folder. One sentence.", "Done."): nobody interrupts, hesitates or says anything a 23-year-old would say, and slow simple sentences from smiling toy figures land in a pre-school register for adults who pay real money for a sports trip, the opposite of the founder's "talks at eye level".

Pacing and length: twelve shots averaging 3.7 s, each built as one line, a pause and a cut, carry 47 spoken words in 44.8 s (about 63 words a minute, with up to a second of dead air inside the first six-word line), so an idea worth 15 to 20 seconds is stretched to 45.

Music: the bed sits roughly 10 dB or more under the voices, is fully out for 5.2 s (16.3-21.5 s) and about 2.4 s (38.8-41.3 s), reaches full level only for the 2.8 s drop and the 2.3 s final hit, and the drop lands on a cat sitting on a book, so the founder's "trendy, fun music" is barely in the film.

There is no sport and no fan truth (no game, crowd, gate, queue or scarf seller; only a ball in a lap and a hoop in the background), and the project's own brief and trend notes (situations travelling fans recognise, one label at most, each film stands alone, no episode numbers) are broken on all four points, because the script was chosen by three machine judges for clarity, feasibility and product truth and none for funny.

A human animator or comedy editor would open on the push or the zip and drop 0-11.9 s, put the plan's title and a page in the picture, make the folder absurdly big, keep both characters in one frame and hold on the reaction, record real voices first and animate to them, cut the air between lines, and finish in 15-25 s with the product shown once at the end.

The three changes that matter most are (1) one self-contained, recognisable sports-trip situation with a visual hook in second one and a real surprise, with no lore and no labels, (2) a human comic performance: real directed voices, two characters sharing the frame, adult conversational speech, and (3) the product once, late and short; what was fine: the cat, Big Yellow, the coral-teal-yellow palette, the push image at 12 s, the top-down suitcase shot, the zip and silence before the cut, the clean render with correct text, the honest product wording, and the planner-versus-improviser pairing.

JOKE BY JOKE (times measured on the no-music file)
1. "No notes. No folder. One sentence." 0.2-3.3 s. A claim, not a joke. Needs season 1.
2. "Nine words. I counted." 4.1-6.0 s. Best line. Buried under the card and played with a grin.
3. "Done." plus four ticks, 6.9 s. A catchphrase a new viewer has never met.
4. "Done? That's MY word!" 9.9-11.5 s. Explains the callback. Said smiling.
5. "I packed one sentence." 12.6-14.1 s. A slogan as a line. The picture is the joke; the label spoils it.
6. "What did I pack?" 16.3 s. Fair set-up.
7. "Maybe... the cat?" 18.0-20.2 s. The cat is in plain view.
8. Open suitcase, 21.5 s. Unreadable without the label.
9. "Step one: say 'Done.'" / "Step two: Luna pushes Big Yellow?!" 24.6-29.3 s. The one real idea: he planned her. Told by reading a closed book aloud. "Big Yellow" is never explained.
10. "Step three: Luna carries the folder." 29.8-32.4 s. Smaller than step two.
11. "My turn. Golf!" / "Golf?" 33.1-39.4 s. Golf is there because the product places golf rounds, not because it is funny.

The pigeon duo I found belongs to an insurance brand and was voiced by two known comedians for about ten years. The sports-lottery duo was built on two actors' voices and mannerisms: one impulsive, one calculating. The snack brand's February 2026 campaign reportedly used AI animation, with its characters beside known performers. I could not confirm an electric-company pigeon campaign. The common thread is a human comic performance behind the mascot. This film has none. Trade reports also say viewers spot generated ads quickly and call them boring or confusing. The hook figures I found come from marketing blogs and are not verified.

On 15 Nov the founder wrote that the "drawn" style (מצויר) works better. This look is sculpted 3D. Ask what they meant.

understand:today.summary: Web search worked, but this session could not open pages, so I rely on search summaries, many from trade or vendor sites. I found no brand whose polished generated cartoon people follow for fun. What people follow is a character with a clear personality inside a cheap, repeatable format: a vlog the character films, a mockumentary talking head, a group-chat serial, a puppet duo. One premise per video, the hook in the first seconds, the brand in the bio or as a cast member. The latest film does the opposite: glossy 3D look, twelve clips, six labels that explain the plot, two product cards. Label generated video everywhere and use only licensed-library or original music.
points: People do not punish generated video as such; they punish video that looks low-effort: in Animoto's 2026 survey (about 450 US consumers and marketers, vendor data) the cues people named were robotic gestures (67%), unnatural voices (55%) and missing emotion (51%), and 36% said an AI video lowers their view of the brand.

The generated series people chose to follow put a character with a personality inside a format that excuses the medium: selfie vlogs 'filmed by' a Bigfoot or a Yeti (since May 2025; about a minute of stitched 8-second clips of everyday chores) and the mockumentary talking heads of Neural Viz, whose creator writes, storyboards and acts every face himself.

Glossy 3D cartoon is the most slop-crowded look on TikTok: Kapwing (data from May 2026) counted 59% AI slop in the first 500 videos shown to a new account and 97 of 100 videos under #cartoonkids, and my reading is that the current art-toy look sits in that neighbourhood.

Brands are judged harder than creators: McDonald's Netherlands pulled a fully generated 45-second Christmas ad three days after launch in December 2025, Coca-Cola's 2024 ad drew the same anger, and an Ad Age discussion of 'Fruit Love Island' (300 million views in nine days, then called slop, mass-reported and stopped) said people accept AI for pure entertainment more than for brand use (I saw this only second-hand).

Counter-evidence: in System1's ad tests viewers did not notice AI unless asked and 18 AI-assisted ads averaged 3.4 stars against 2.3 for all ads (a small, biased sample), while its 2026 Super Bowl review said the weak ads lacked a story and a character to root for.

The brand characters people follow for fun (Duolingo's owl, Ryanair's talking plane, Scrub Daddy, Nutter Butter) post quick lo-fi bits built on current trends, the character is a personality and the product is rarely pitched; Crocs launched a mascot in 2026 that does not speak at all.

The 2025-2026 shift is from single posts to small shows: 'Roomies' from the fintech Bilt (an ultra-short sitcom with the brand named only in the bio, two Webby People's Voice awards in 2026), 'The Group Chat' (one creator plays every part, roughly 100 million views over five episodes) and 'The Chit Show' (a million followers in a month off one catchphrase).

Comedy that builds a following is one premise per video plus a repeatable bit, meaning a fixed setup, a recurring character and a line the audience waits for, and platforms now support it with series tools (TikTok mini-dramas for brands since June 2026, Meta testing 'Series').

Hook: TikTok's own ad guidance says to put the hook inside the first six seconds and reports that 90% of ad-recall impact falls there, another TikTok guide says three seconds, and third-party claims of one to two seconds are unverified.

Length: there is no agreed best length; Socialinsider's 2026 benchmark has videos under 30 seconds winning on engagement while longer ones collect more views, sketch creators run from about 20 to 90 seconds, and for an account with no followers I judge 10 to 30 seconds the safer start.

Captions: estimates of sound-off viewing run from 60% to 90% and are poorly sourced, so spoken words should be burned in, but a label that explains the plot (the latest film has six) shows the joke does not carry itself (my judgement).

Handmade is the late-2026 counter-trend: Levi's made a stop-motion film that took about 2,000 hours, Barbour and Thatchers went to Aardman, a Canva report says 78% prefer ads made by people, Gartner (1,006 US consumers) found 65% think brands publish too much AI content, and TikTok's 2026 trend report favours real experience over 'curated perfection'.

Sports fans: what travelled in 2026 was the experience around the match (matchday and away-day vlogs, groundhopping, fan reactions), for example a German fan rating American food stops out of ten on his World Cup road trip (about 360,000 to 400,000 followers on X, millions of views), and a KAYAK survey says 84% have had a group trip die in the planning stage, which is this product's natural joke.

Closest precedents for the founder's presenter-duo idea: Israel's electric company has used the puppet pair Sheka and Teka for more than twenty years, Bissli brought its cartoon characters back in February 2026 next to young creators, and the small shoe brand KANE signed an AI Yeti vlogger as its 'athlete' (439,000 followers by one report); I could not find the 'pigeons' or Toto campaigns by search.

AI labels: TikTok requires a label on realistic generated content, may remove unlabelled posts, reads C2PA tags and since November 2025 lets users turn AI content down; Meta requires its label for photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio but not for cartoon style; YouTube asks for disclosure, has auto-detected and labelled since May 2026, shows the label for stylised animation only in the description, and has demonetised and in some cases terminated mass-produced 'inauthentic' channels.

Music: a TikTok business account may use only the Commercial Music Library, that licence does not cover reposting on other platforms, and record labels have sued brands over songs in social posts (Marriott, Chili's, Crumbl, DSW, and Quince in April 2026), so 'trendy music' has to mean library tracks or original music.
understand:today.details:
FIVE FORMATS MOST LIKELY TO WORK (my judgement from the evidence)
1. The character's own vlog. Luna holds the camera on a sports trip and rates each stop out of ten while Timo's plan disagrees: 15-25 seconds, one or two unbroken shots, one joke. It is the best-proven liked generated format, and a hand-held selfie hides stiff motion.
2. Mockumentary confessionals. Each of the two tells an unseen interviewer what happened on the same trip, and the cut between the two versions is the joke. Two fixed framings are reused every episode, so the script can be finished on paper before any credit is spent.
3. The group chat that never becomes a trip. Message bubbles and short reaction shots follow friends failing to plan a match weekend, and in some episodes one typed sentence puts a plan on the table. Most of the picture is text, so it is cheap and little of it can look generated.
4. A puppet or clay-look duo on one fixed set. Two seats in a stand, 10-20 seconds of banter, one gag, the same frame every time: the nearest thing to the founder's Israeli presenter-duo references. Evidence for generated puppet looks is thin; real hand puppets filmed on a phone are the safest version.
5. Flat 2D cartoon gags. Simple drawn characters, little movement, one gag in 10-20 seconds, several a week, as Chikn Nuggit does. A flat drawn look reads as made by a person and stays consistent more easily than glossy 3D.

FIVE THINGS TO AVOID
1. The glossy 3D toy look with talking close-ups and synthetic voices: it matches the cues people name as AI.
2. A plot that needs explaining labels, several twists in 45 seconds, season numbers on an account with no audience.
3. A product card with ticks in every film; keep the brand in the handle, the bio and an occasional punchline.
4. Sincere or realistic-human generated scenes, and any generated video posted without the platform's AI label.
5. Chart songs, club or league names, borrowed TV formats, and many near-identical posts.

understand:craft-cost.summary: The last film cost 47 dollars through habit: about 190 paid seconds of clips for a 45-second film. The same service sells an 8-second Veo 3.1 lite clip for 0.30 and a still for 0.022. A 15-25 second sketch can cost 0.7 to 3.2 dollars if work goes sound first, stills second, motion last, one take per shot. The glossy 3D toy look sits near the "shouts AI" end; cut-out moved in the edit, felt or clay puppets on twos, and a phone vlog hide the tells best. Voices: real people or a dialogue model, no lip-sync on rigid faces. A test of at most 1.6 dollars proves the look first. Web evidence is thin, mostly vendor blogs.
points: Under a quarter of the paid footage reached the screen: 45 dollars at 0.235 a second is about 190 seconds of clips and the edit uses about 42 of them, because every shot was filmed twice at 1080p on the dearest model.

The work order that saves most: write the sketch, record or generate the voices, cut an animatic from stills with the final sound for under half a dollar, and buy a moving clip only for a shot the animatic shows needs motion.

The present glossy 3D toy look sits near the "shouts AI" end: smooth plastic skin, soft perfect light and slow smooth motion are the default output of image models, and clean surfaces hide no drift and no lip error.

Best at hiding the tells, in order: cut-out or paper collage moved in the edit (no generated motion at all), felt, clay or puppet stop-motion stepped to 12 frames a second, then a phone vlog held by the character; a flat 2D cartoon is safe only when the edit moves it, since video models make its lines wobble.
The founder's own words point the same way: on 15 Nov they wrote that the drawn style works better, and on 12 Nov that Veo is better (the word before "veo" in that message is unclear).

Price facts from my free checks today: Veo 3.1 lite image-to-video costs 0.30 at 720p whether the clip is 4, 6 or 8 seconds, about six times cheaper per second than the Kling 4.0 1080p setting, and Veo 3.1 fast costs 0.60.

Voices, option one, costs nothing and is the only truly real one: two people record the lines on a phone; a May 2026 Gallup-Bentley survey of 3,270 US adults found that 73% of those aged 18-29 call AI-made people or voices in ads unacceptable.

Voices, option two: a dialogue speech model (0.0044 dollars for two lines) gives five readings of each line for cents so the funniest can be chosen, but adding lip-sync costs 0.04 to 0.50 a shot and is risky, because one sync vendor's own help pages say cartoon faces are generally not supported.

Voices, option three: Veo's own speech is rated more natural than Kling's in the comparisons I found and its lips match by construction at no extra cost, but a report says the voice changes from clip to clip, so each character should speak in one clip only; a narrator or voice-over over flap mouths, hidden mouths or backs avoids lips altogether for cents.

Recipe A, cut-out, about 0.7 dollars: 5 to 7 set-ups from about 18 stills, no video model, pose swaps, snaps and two or three mouth shapes moved in the edit, voices from people or the dialogue model; a still is redrawn only for a named defect, at most two rounds.

Recipe B, felt puppets on twos, about 1.5 dollars: 5 shots of which 3 are Veo 3.1 lite 8-second clips at 720p from start stills, re-timed to 12 frames a second and upscaled in the edit, voice-over with no lip-sync, one take per shot and one retake budgeted for the whole video.

Recipe C, character vlog with native voice, about 3.2 dollars (1.7 with lite): 3 Veo 3.1 fast 8-second clips at 720p, one speaker per clip talking to a hand-held phone, one take per shot and two retakes budgeted.

Against the expensive way all three lose 1080p sharpness, the choice between two takes, and reference-locked faces and voices, so actions must stay small and frontal; A also loses fluid motion and true lip-sync, and Veo lite's quality in these styles is untested.

Retake rule for every recipe: only for a defect on a written list (wrong character or prop, morphing, a cut inside the clip, wrong words) that the edit cannot hide, only after the start still or the prompt has been changed, once per shot, and a second failure turns the shot into a still with voice-over.

First test, at most 1.6 dollars: one 8-second joke as three style stills, five voice readings plus a phone recording, the cut-out version, one Veo lite clip, one Veo fast clip with a spoken line and one lip-sync probe, judged against pass rules written beforehand; a person must judge the voice sample because the assistant cannot hear, and apart from that nothing goes to the founder until a video is finished, as they asked.

Process rules: a written cap of 6 dollars per video checked before every paid call, one take by default (the "--takes 2" habit is in the skill file and the season notes, not in the code), every fixable thing fixed on 0.022 stills first, a free price check before each batch, and a "paid seconds on screen" figure reported with every delivery (last film about 22%, target above 70%).

create:mascots.name: Tip & Dent
create:mascots.logline: Two traffic cones stand outside every big game in the world, facing the wrong way, and say what they think of every fan who arrives.
create:mascots.why_this_is_what_the_founder_means:
What matches the founder's own words:
- 15 Nov: "the presenters, the duo and the face" of the brand, like the campaigns they named. Those are pairs of non-human characters who stand at the side of ordinary life and comment on it. Two cones at the gate are the same class. They are not birds, so they do not copy the pigeons.
- "International, humorous and nice, at eye level." The cones talk like two adults who have seen everything. The camera sits on the ground at their height. Nobody presents to the lens.
- 15 Nov: "interactions between the characters". Both are in one frame for the whole film and they talk to each other.
- 17 Nov: "authentic". The cones have never seen a game. They only see people arriving. That is the brand's side of the gate too: the trip, not the match. Every joke is something a travelling fan has lived: the friend who organised it, the partner who was not told, the landing an hour before the start.
- 17 Nov: "not as if made with AI". There is no face, no mouth, no hand and no readable sign for a model to get wrong. By default no video model is used.
- 17 Nov, cost: about 1 dollar an episode against about 47 for the last film.
- "Start over on everything": nothing from the earlier films is used.

Where it does not match, said plainly:
- On 15 Nov the founder named Timo and Luna themselves. This drops them. Only the founder can say if "everything" includes them.
- On 15 Nov they wrote that the drawn style works better. This is a tabletop stop-motion look, not a drawing.
- They asked for "adventures". Cones cannot go anywhere. A van moves them to a new sport each time. That is the only adventure.
- The brand is carried by one spoken phrase and a 2.5-second plate. That is less brand than the reference campaigns show.
create:mascots.cast:
Timo and Luna are replaced, not kept. Reasons: the job was new mascots from nothing; two toy-like humans need faces, hands and lips, which is where generated video fails; and their humour needed earlier episodes. This is my call for this pitch. The founder decides.

TIP. A tall, new, bright orange cone. One white band, square black base, perfect point. Two googly eyes set close together, small pupils. He believes cones run the event and that a plan on paper always works. He talks fast, in rules and times. He panics. Things land on him.

DENT. Shorter, faded, the point bent over, one big dent in his side, a strip of silver tape, a few old stickers. Eyes wide apart, one a little bigger, big pupils, lids half closed. A team bus ran him over once and he counts it as meeting the team. He talks slowly, in five words or fewer. He says the true thing. Nothing surprises him.

Neither has a mouth, arms, legs or eyebrows. All the acting is eyes, a hop, a tilt and the voice.

Why they are funny together: Tip asks, Dent answers. Tip trusts the timetable, Dent knows what happens to people. They are fond of each other and never say so.

Rules of their world. They cannot move. They cannot turn round. The game is always behind them, so they have been outside hundreds of games and seen none. They work out everything from sound. People cannot hear them. A van drops them at a new sport each time.

THE FANS. Seen only from the thigh down. Heard off screen. New each episode.

KEV. Never seen. In most episodes somebody, somewhere, is shouting for Kev.

Stickers: Tip with a sheet of paper on his face. Dent on his side. Both looking the same way. "Could've been one sentence."
create:mascots.look:
A tabletop stop-motion look, as if built on a desk.
- The cones look like hand-rolled plasticine with thumbprints. The eyes are craft googly eyes.
- The set looks like painted cardboard and model gravel: a stadium wall, a gate, floodlights, plain flags. All of it out of focus. No words, badges or numbers anywhere.
- The world uses the brand's colours without a logo: cream ground, racing-green wall and doors, brass light, oxblood flags. The cones are the only orange.
- The fans are puppet legs: felt trousers, clay shoes. The frame cuts them at the thigh.
- Vertical 9:16. The camera is locked on the ground at cone height, close, with shallow focus. The cones fill the lower half. Legs pass behind and between them, never in front.
- Movement is stepped, 12 pictures a second, with a slight light flicker.

Why it should read as made by hand:
- Each cone is one picture file, made once and reused in every episode. It cannot drift.
- The eyes are drawn by the edit, not by a model. They are the same in every frame of every episode.
- The edit moves the pieces. No video model moves them. So nothing floats or morphs.
- There are no faces, hands, lips or signs, which is where the usual tells show.
- Captions are the only text, one at a time, in one type style.

Honest limits. The stills are still generated; this imitates handmade work. This look has not been tested with this image model. If the test fails, the same scripts can be shot for real: two toy cones, stick-on eyes and a phone on the ground outside a real venue, filming legs only. No other concept I know of has that way out.
create:mascots.voices_and_sound:
Voices carry about nine tenths of this. There are no faces to help.
- Tip: quick, precise, a little too loud. Dent: low, slow, dry, warm. Both adults. No cartoon voices.
- Best option, free: two funny real people record all lines together on a phone, so they can talk over each other. Second option: the dialogue speech model, five readings of each exchange, pick the best (about 10 cents an episode).
- There are no mouths, so no lip-sync is ever bought. Voices can be recast late. A Hebrew dub costs cents.
- Sound first. Voices, crowd and effects are cut to final timing as a radio version before any picture is made. If the radio version is not funny, the episode stops there.
- A person must listen to the voices. I cannot hear. This is the one thing in the process that needs a human ear before a film is finished.
- Words are checked by speech-to-text read-back against the script.

The sound of the place does the "authentic" work: crowd through a wall, footsteps, wheels on concrete, a far-off announcer with no words. In every episode a roar or a buzzer comes from the game the cones cannot see.

Fixed closing sound: two knocks on a hollow cone, "tonk-tonk". Then the plate.

Music: a short bouncy loop, low under the talk, full for the last 2.5 seconds. It must come from a library a business account may use, or be original. Chart songs cannot be used legally, so "trendy" has to mean the style, not the song.

Captions: every spoken line, one at a time, above whoever speaks. Nothing else on screen until the plate.
create:mascots.episode_engine:
One episode, every time:
1. Second zero: something physical happens at cone height (legs burst through, a wheel screams past, eyes spin). A line is spoken inside the first second and a half.
2. One fan, couple or group arrives. That is the only situation.
3. Tip reads it wrong or asks. Dent says the true thing.
4. Something from the human world lands on or beside a cone.
5. A sound comes from the game behind them. They cannot turn.
6. Dent's last two words are always "one sentence".
7. Tonk-tonk. The plate, 2.5 seconds. Cut.
12 to 25 seconds. A new sport each time. Each one works alone.

Ten more:
1. Four Days Early (football). A lone fan drums outside an empty ground. It is Tuesday. The game is Saturday. "He thinks he's early." "He is early."
2. Which Cones (football). Two friends are both on the phone shouting "I'm by the cones!" They are at two different stadiums in the same city.
3. Quiet, Please (tennis). Everyone whispers. A fan tries to tiptoe a suitcase with a squealing wheel past the queue. Even the last line is whispered.
4. The Clubs (football). A calm fan walks past a football ground with golf clubs. Tip thinks he is at the wrong sport. Dent: "Golf this morning. Football tonight." Tip: "You can do two?"
5. The Car Park People (American football). Fans bring chairs and a grill six hours early and stay in the car park on purpose. Tip, close to tears: "They came for us."
6. This Is The Sport (a city run). Thousands of legs sprint past. Tip screams that everyone is late. Dent: "It's a run. This is the sport." Tip: "We're in one?"
7. Gary (football, night). A clean circle on the ground where a third cone stood. Singing fans took him. "He's a lamp in a student flat now." Dent would love to be taken.
8. Same Twenty Cars (motorsport). Tip thinks it is terrible traffic. "It's the same twenty cars, Tip. For two hours." A fan arrives on foot, in flip-flops, from the city the race is named after.
9. Beach (football, family). A dad, a mum and a child with a bucket. "You said beach." "There is a beach. It's near the second stadium."
10. The Van (closer). Dark, engine noise, both cones lying on their sides. "Where next?" "Nobody tells us." "Nine hundred games." "And never one sentence."

Honest note: 5 and 7 are pure character. The brand is only the plate there. I would allow about one of those in five.
create:mascots.where_the_brand_sits:
Three places, and nowhere else.
1. Spoken, once: Dent's last two words are "one sentence". In mess episodes: "Could've been one sentence." In the rare calm episode a fan says it ("It took one sentence") and Dent repeats it.
2. Shown, once: after the tonk-tonk a single plate rises between the cones for 2.5 seconds. The V crest, VENUVOY, and the sign-off the fact sheet already cleared: "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." The cones stay in the picture and look at it. No ticks, no feature list, no typing.
3. Worn: one of the old stickers on Dent is the round green-and-brass V crest. No words. Fans really do sticker everything near a ground.
Also the account name and the bio.

Truth rules for the writing:
- "One sentence" is short for the real thing: the sentence fills the planner, the traveller checks it and presses Create plans. The films compress this, as the cleared sign-off does. The page the viewer lands on must not promise more.
- The mess in an episode may only be one a plan would fix: the day and time of a real fixture, the order of the days, getting around, when you can land and still make the game, more than one sport in a trip.
- Never a mess about buying a ticket, a sold-out game, a flight search or a hotel choice. Venuvoy does not book or sell anything and promises no tickets. The word is "plans".
- No club, league, stadium or city names. No casinos in these films. Golf to play and stadium tours exist only in England; runs and hikes only in nine European countries.

scripts.title: Fun Ends (football, dusk)
scripts.script:
SET. Outside a football ground an hour before kick-off, dusk. Camera locked on the ground at cone height. Tip left of centre, Dent right of centre. Behind them, out of focus: green stadium wall, floodlight glow, plain flags.
TEXT ON SCREEN. Each spoken line as one caption above whoever speaks, one at a time. Nothing else until the plate.

0.0-2.5 MASTER. HOOK, first second: eight pairs of legs burst across behind the cones, right to left, packed tight. The front pair walks backwards, facing the others, papers flapping. Both cones' pupils snap right and follow the pack across together.
ORGANISER (off, hoarse, from the first frame): "Stay together! Kev. KEV! Not that gate!"
The pack is gone. One sheet of paper hangs in the air.

2.5-5.4 MASTER.
TIP (still looking after them): "Which one planned the trip?"
DENT (not looking): "The one not having fun."
ORGANISER (far away, small): "KEV!"

5.4-7.2 MASTER. The sheet drops in three steps and slaps flat over Tip's face. Sound: paper slap. Tip rocks back. Dent's pupils slide over to him. Hold. Nobody speaks.

7.2-13.0 CLOSER on the two of them (same picture, scaled up).
DENT: "What is it?"
TIP (muffled; the paper puffs on each word): "It's a spreadsheet."
TIP: "'Four p.m.: fun.'"
DENT (touched): "Aw."
TIP: "'Four fifteen: fun ends.'"   <- PUNCHLINE
Hold 0.6 s. Dent's pupils drift to the lens. Lids half closed.

13.0-16.2 MASTER. A huge roar from inside the ground. The floodlight glow jumps. Neither cone can turn round. The paper peels off Tip and blows away.
DENT (flat): "Could've been one sentence."   <- BUTTON

16.2-19.0 MASTER. Sound: tonk-tonk. One plate rises low between the cones: V crest, VENUVOY, "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." No caption now. Both cones look down at it, then at each other. Very far off: "...Kev?"
LAST IMAGE: two cones looking at each other over the plate, the ground glowing behind them.

36 spoken words. The paper lands blank side out. No writing is ever seen.

scripts.title: Romantic Weekend (motorsport, day)
scripts.script:
SET. Outside a race circuit gate, bright day. Behind the cones, out of focus: the back of a grandstand, a fence, plain flags. Cars are heard, never seen. Every pass (NEEEOOOWM) spins both cones' pupils one full turn and shakes the picture a little.
TEXT ON SCREEN. Each spoken line as one caption, one at a time. The couple's captions sit by their legs. Nothing else until the plate.

0.0-0.8 MASTER. HOOK, first second: NEEEOOOWM. Four pupils spin. Two pairs of legs stop dead between the cones: his in clean white trainers, hers in boots, a folding chair under her arm. His weekend bag drops to the ground.

0.8-3.6
HIM (off, flat): "You said 'romantic weekend.'"
HER (off, bright): "It IS a romantic weekend!"

3.6-4.8 NEEEOOOWM. Pupils spin. Settle.

4.8-7.2
HER: "...It's a very romantic racetrack."
TIP (whisper, eyes sliding to Dent): "It isn't."

7.2-11.0
HIM: "And tomorrow?"
HER (small): "...More cars."
HIM: "When did you even plan this?"
HER: "It took one sentence!"

11.0-14.4 His legs turn and walk out left. His bag stays. NEEEOOOWM. Spin.
TIP: "That's it. He's gone."
DENT (eyes on the bag): "He left his bag."

14.4-17.8 His legs walk back in and stop beside hers. A pause.
HIM (quiet): "...Which one are we cheering for?"
HER: "The fast one."   <- PUNCHLINE

17.8-18.6
DENT (dry, impressed): "One sentence."   <- BUTTON

18.6-21.0 Sound: tonk-tonk. The plate rises between the cones: V crest, VENUVOY, "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." No caption now. The cones look down at it. One last NEEEOOOWM. Their pupils spin.
LAST IMAGE: the plate between two cones with spinning eyes, and four feet side by side behind them.

49 spoken words. She is the fan and he is the one who was not told. That is on purpose.

scripts.title: A Whole Hour (basketball, night)
scripts.script:
SET. Outside an indoor arena at night. Wet ground. Warm light from glass doors behind the cones, out of focus. Through the wall: squeaking shoes, a bouncing ball, a crowd.
TEXT ON SCREEN. Each spoken line as one caption above whoever speaks, one at a time. Nothing else until the plate.

0.0-1.5 MASTER. HOOK, first second: a suitcase wheel screams across, right to left, legs sprinting, an airline tag whipping on the handle. Both cones' pupils snap and follow.
TIP: "Late."

1.5-3.6
DENT: "Straight from the airport. Tag's still on the bag."

3.6-5.4 Through the wall: BZZZT.
TIP: "End of the first quarter."

5.4-7.1 The legs and the suitcase sprint back, left to right. Pupils follow.
DENT: "Wrong door."

7.1-8.5 BZZZT.
TIP: "Half-time."

8.5-12.0 The legs come through a third time, slower. The wheel now goes clack, clack, clack.
TIP (upset for him): "He landed at seven. Game's at eight. That's a whole hour!"

12.0-14.4
DENT: "That works if the plane lands on the court."   <- PUNCHLINE

14.4-16.4 One suitcase wheel rolls in on its own. It slows and tips over against Tip's base. Tik. Both cones look down at it. BZZZT.

16.4-17.8
DENT: "Could've been one sentence."   <- BUTTON

17.8-20.3 Sound: tonk-tonk. The plate rises between the cones: V crest, VENUVOY, "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." No caption now. The cones look at it. Tip looks back down at the wheel.
LAST IMAGE: the plate, two cones, one small wheel lying against Tip.

44 spoken words. What is true here: with your landing time, the plan shows the latest you can land and still make the game. It does not find or book the flight, and the film does not say it does.

create:mascots.recipe:
This is the cut-out recipe from the craft brief. Prices are the ones in that brief. I did not recheck them and I generated nothing.

Order of work:
1. Script on paper. Read it aloud to two or three people. No smile, no episode. Cost 0.
2. Voices. Two real people on a phone (free), or the dialogue speech model with five readings of each exchange (about 0.10).
3. Radio version: voices, crowd and effects at final timing. Words checked by read-back. A person listens. This is the gate before any picture.
4. Stills, 0.022 each.
 - Once for the whole series: Tip in 4 poses and Dent in 4 poses, in day light and night light. 16 stills plus up to 8 redraws, about 0.53. Backgrounds removed in code.
 - Per episode: 1 background, 6 to 10 pieces (legs in two walk poses, a bag, a sheet of paper, a wheel), up to 5 redraws. 12 to 16 stills, about 0.35.
5. The edit builds the film at 12 pictures a second. It slides, hops, tilts and swaps the pieces. It draws the googly eyes, the lids, the captions and the plate. A closer shot is the same picture scaled up.
6. Video model only by exception. At most one Veo 3.1 lite clip, 8 seconds, 720p, 0.30, for a movement the pieces cannot fake. None is planned in these three scripts. The cones are laid over the clip afterwards, so the model never draws them.
7. Music and effects, about 0.15.

Shots: one locked master and one closer view per episode, 5 to 7 beats.
Takes: one. A still is redrawn only for a named defect, at most two rounds. A clip is retaken once, only after the still or the prompt has changed. A second failure turns it back into moved pieces.

Sum per episode: 0.35 stills, 0.10 voices, 0.15 music and effects. About 0.60. With one clip and one retake, about 1.20. The written cap stays 6 dollars and is checked before every paid call. The series kit costs about 0.53 once.

create:mascots.risks:
Plainly:
1. It may feel dumb to the founder. They wrote "everything feels dumb" and asked for "the highest level". Two cones with googly eyes are simple on purpose. If the dry adult writing does not carry it, this reads as a children's clip.
2. It drops Timo and Luna, whom the founder named as the faces of the brand on 15 Nov. If "start over" did not mean them, this pitch is wrong at the root.
3. It is not drawn. On 15 Nov they said the drawn style works better.
4. Everything rests on the voices. With no faces, a flat voice kills it. I cannot hear, so a person must judge. Real people are the safe choice; machine voices are the weak point.
5. The cones cannot do anything. If nothing physical happens every three seconds it becomes a picture with talking. No mouths also means a viewer with the sound off depends on captions and hops to know who speaks.
6. The stage that moves the pieces is not built. The first episode costs working time, and done badly it looks like a slideshow, not stop-motion.
7. The handmade look is an imitation and is untested. Walking legs are the hardest part to fake.
8. The brand link is thin. People may like the cones and not remember the brand. The cones never use the product.
9. "Could've been one sentence" promises a little more than the product does. The sentence fills the planner and the traveller still presses Create plans. Nothing is booked. In "A Whole Hour" the landing time is something the traveller enters.
10. Cones are not ownable. Anyone can use a cone. My two quick searches found single cone accounts (Cony, Mr. Coni) and a 2002 British cartoon called Cone Control, and no cone duo for a brand. I read search summaries only. The names are not legally checked.
11. Two football-gate ideas in a row would feel the same. The sport must really change each time.
12. The jokes are untested on people. I think "the one not having fun", "fun ends" and "the fast one" are real laughs. "A Whole Hour" is the weakest of the three. Nothing here guarantees it catches on, and the account starts with no followers.
13. Off-screen fans add one or two voices per episode, which adds to risk 4.
14. Platform rules still apply: label generated content where the platform asks, and use only library or original music.

create:duo.name: One Sentence, Timo.
create:duo.logline: Two paper friends on sports trips: Timo is always sure, Luna is always right, and every twenty-second mess ends with her saying "One sentence, Timo."
create:duo.why_this_is_what_the_founder_means:
I read every message. This is how the concept answers their own words.

- 15 Nov 14:43, the clearest one: Timo and Luna as "the presenters, the duo and the face", in "adventures, comic things", like the Israeli ad duos, "only ours international, humorous and nice, at eye level". This is that form and nothing else: two fixed characters, one situation, a quick bicker, one punchline, and the brand signs it with one fixed line and one fixed sound.
- 15 Nov 06:10: "the drawn style works better" and "interactions between the characters". Cut paper is drawn. The two share one frame for almost the whole film and talk over each other. The last film had no shot with two speakers.
- 16 Nov: "consistent, clean... animation, not cheap AI". The same paper pieces are used in every frame of every episode, so nothing can drift. No video model moves the characters.
- 17 Nov: "authentic, funny, nice, fun to watch, not as if made with AI". Each film is a moment a travelling fan has lived or fears: the empty ground, the red light at the gate, being shushed. It is written as talk, not as copy. Luna teases him and always has his back.
- 17 Nov on money and on showing work: about 70 cents a film against 47 dollars, and nothing is shown until it is finished.
- 15 Nov 15:34: more than football. The first three films are football, tennis (with baseball next day) and basketball.
- "Plot", in their mouth, means a story you follow at once. Each film is one place, one problem, in real time. No earlier episode is needed.

Two things only the founder can answer, each in one word. Neither changes the scripts. (1) Does "start over on everything" include the names Timo and Luna? (2) Did "drawn" mean flat and drawn, or only "animated, not real people"?

Where I may be wrong: I am reading their taste from four messages and a list of TV campaigns. Those campaigns are polished. Cut paper is deliberately simple. If they picture television-grade mascots, this may look too modest to them. I say more under risks.
create:duo.cast:
KEPT: the names Timo and Luna, tall and short, his teal and her coral. The founder chose these names for "the duo and the face" on 15 Nov, and names cost nothing.
REPLACED: the bodies, the world and the temperaments. The old planner-against-improviser pairing made Timo stiff and made every joke the same one: her sentence beats his plan. The cat and the yellow suitcase are retired. They may sit in a background as paper props, never as plot. If the founder wants new names too, swap them; nothing depends on them.

TIMO, the hot one. The friend who says "trust me, I'll sort it". All heart, no admin. Loud, quick, sure, wrong. Football is his measure of everything, so every other sport confuses him. He never admits a mistake; he gives it a new name ("It's early." "Red is thinking."). He talks in bursts and starts sentences before he has finished thinking. He is never mean. He bought the tea.
Design: tall narrow head in teal card, round eyes that are always wide open, one thick eyebrow, a big jaw on a brass pin, a tuft of black paper curls.

LUNA, the cool one. Dry, low, slow. She speaks in short lines, mostly three to seven words. She states facts; she does not make jokes. She never repeats herself and never raises her voice. She looks at her tea or her phone more than at him. She lets him walk into it because she finds it funny, and she always has the second ticket in her pocket.
Design: short, round head in coral card, heavy half-closed eyelids, a small jaw, a straight fringe.

Not human skin colours, so nothing uncanny and no question of who is what. You can tell who is who with the sound off: his eyes are always wide, hers are always half shut.
Both wear one scarf, racing green and cream, the brand's colours. It is an invented team. It is the only branding before the last three seconds.

WHY THEY ARE FUNNY TOGETHER. He builds a tower of confidence; she takes out one brick. He is loud about small things; she is quiet about big ones ("Where we live."). He gives her ten words; she gives back two.

RULES OF THE DOUBLE ACT
1. Timo is sure. Luna is right. He is never mean, she is never smug.
2. Always side by side in one frame, Timo left, Luna right. They look at each other. Timo looks at us once, at the end.
3. One place, one problem, real time. No narrator, no labels, no flashbacks, nothing from an earlier film.
4. Timo never says "I was wrong". Luna never explains twice.
5. They interrupt. Lines may overlap.
6. The last spoken words are always Luna's: "One sentence, Timo." Then the whistle and the sign.
7. A new sport or a new part of a sports trip each time.
8. About one film in five, Luna loses her cool or Timo's way wins, so it does not go stale.
9. If a joke needs a label, the joke is rewritten.
create:duo.look:
A POP-UP BOOK OF SPORTS TRIPS, made of cut paper and card.

In concrete words:
- The characters are flat paper puppets about a hand tall. Each is a few pieces: head, jaw, body, two arms, eyes, eyebrow. The pieces are joined with visible brass split-pins at the jaw and shoulders.
- You can see the paper: grain, slightly uneven scissor edges, a pencil line left here and there, a soft shadow under every piece.
- Each place is a card diorama in four or five layers that pops up like a page of a pop-up book in the first third of a second. That pop is the series' opening move.
- The paper world uses the brand's own colours: cream card, racing green, brass pins, a little oxblood. The two characters are the teal and the coral.
- Crowds are rows of paper people with heads on pins. A whole crowd can turn at once by flipping.
- Every place has its own light: a grey afternoon, a white tennis noon, a night arena with warm doors. Never one sunset for everything.
- Movement is pose to pose, twelve poses a second. Jaws flap to the real voice. Heads tilt, arms swing on their pins, a head turn is a card flip. When Luna says nothing, nothing moves. Holds are held.
- The camera does not move. A very small flicker in the light, as in stop-motion.
- Text: each spoken line on a cream paper strip beside the speaker, one at a time (a teal tab for Timo, a coral tab for Luna). Then the sign at the end. Nothing else, ever. In-world screens show a red cross or a green tick, never words.

WHY IT WILL READ AS MADE BY HAND
1. No video model moves anything. So the cues people name for AI video (floating motion, shapes that melt, lips that drift) cannot happen. Every move is a keyframe placed against the recorded voice. That is how cut-out animation has always been made.
2. The look and the method agree. The characters are flat pieces and they move like flat pieces. Nothing pretends to be three-dimensional.
3. The same pieces are reused, so the characters are identical in every frame and every episode.
4. All text is typeset in the edit, so it is always correct.
5. Stepped timing, holds and snaps are choices. Generated video floats evenly; this does not.
6. Real voices (see voices).

HONEST LIMITS
- The paper pieces are still generated pictures. A trained eye may notice the finish. Pieces get one pass to add flaws and are kept simple.
- A handmade material is no protection by itself. Search summaries today show felt, clay and yarn looks are already sold as AI video filters. What protects this series is hand-set motion, human voices and writing, not paper.
- It is not smooth. On 16 Nov the founder used the word "smooth". I take that to mean no glitches. If they meant fluid motion, this look is wrong for them.
- The designs can be built as real paper or felt puppets later, for a stadium meet-up or a filmed sketch, if the series earns it.

Fallback if "paper" tests badly: the same pieces and the same scripts in flat felt applique. The seven-cent style frames decide.
create:duo.voices_and_sound:
VOICES COME FIRST, AND THEY SHOULD BE HUMAN.
Every duo the founder named is remembered for its voices. So:
- Two people record each sketch together: one phone between them, a quiet room, eight run-throughs of the whole twenty seconds, talking over each other. They mark the take that made them laugh. Cost: nothing.
- Timo: quick, warm, a little hoarse, always on the front foot. Luna: low, slow, dry, never raises her voice. Light non-native accents are welcome. No accent is played for laughs.
- The film is then animated to that take. The timing of the voices is the timing of the film.
- I cannot hear. No voice should be chosen by me. The performers choose, or one other person does.

FALLBACK if no two people can be found: a dialogue speech model (0.0044 dollars for two lines in the craft brief). Five readings of the whole sketch, a person picks. Its documentation, as summarised in search results, says it handles interruptions and whisper tags. I have not tested that. I expect whispers and overlaps to be the weak spots.

NO LIP-SYNC MODEL. A paper jaw on a pin opens with the loudness of the voice. That costs nothing and suits the look.

HEBREW LATER: record a Hebrew take, the jaws follow by themselves, swap the sign text. No new animation, no credits.

SOUND
- No music under the talk. Jokes die under a music bed. Each place has its own sound: wind in an empty ground, the hush before a serve, an arena concourse. Small paper sounds for the moves.
- The fixed sound: the referee's full-time whistle, three blasts, then a two-second original sting (terrace claps and one small brass hit). The same in every film.
- The founder asked for trendy music. Honest answer: a chart song is not allowed on a business account, and brands have been sued for it. If they want it, a track from the platform's commercial library can be added at upload, low, on that platform only. The whistle and sting stay ours.
create:duo.episode_engine:
THE SHAPE, 18 to 22 seconds, the same every time
1. 0 to 2 s. The page pops up on a picture that is already wrong, with one sound. No title, no logo. This is the hook.
2. 2 to 8 s. Timo explains why it is fine. Luna answers in a few words.
3. 8 to 14 s. One new fact turns it: worse than we thought, or better in a way he ruins.
4. 14 to 18 s. Timo's small human line. This is the laugh.
5. Last 3 s. Luna: "One sentence, Timo." The sign pops up, the whistle blows, Timo looks at us.

Two flavours, taken in turn. "Timo sorted it": it went wrong and her line is a rebuke. "Luna typed it": the trip is fine, Timo is the problem, and her line is the answer to his question.

TEN MORE, one line each
1. WRONG END (football). The goal goes in and Timo is the only one on his feet, in the home end; he turns his scarf inside out and sings their song without knowing one word. (Brand: the sign only.)
2. LAP ONE (motorsport). Both heads whip left to right as the cars pass in half a second. "Who was that?" "All of them." "We came for THAT?" "That was practice." "They PRACTISE?" (The plan covers the whole race weekend.)
3. FIVE K (a Saturday-morning run). Timo runs in his scarf and is overtaken by a pram, then a dog. "I came to WATCH sport." "It's in the plan." "Who typed 'run'?" (True only in the countries where the planner places runs.)
4. ONE PIE (any sport). Eighty minutes of nil-nil, he leaves for one pie, the roar comes through the wall; he runs back and the second roar comes while he is in the tunnel. (Sign only.)
5. EASY PACE (the three plans). "What kind of person picks 'Easy Pace'?" Day three, game four: Timo has no voice left and is held up by his scarf. He croaks: "...easy pace." (The plan names are real: Big Matches, Balanced, Easy Pace.)
6. FORE (a golf round, London or Manchester only). Timo sinks a putt, knee-slides across the green and pulls his shirt over his head. Silence. "Where's the keeper?"
7. BODY CLOCK (basketball in the US). Tip-off. Timo is asleep bolt upright with the foam finger still raised. "It's 3 a.m. in my legs." He wakes at the final buzzer shouting "GOAL!"
8. BOTH TEAMS (football). Timo proudly buys a half-and-half scarf. Every paper fan in the street stops and turns. "It's got BOTH teams!" "Exactly." (Sign only.)
9. THE MANAGER (stadium tour, England, never on a match day). Timo sits in the manager's seat in the empty dugout and makes a substitution. The guide: "Sir. The tour left ten minutes ago."
10. NO CLOCK (baseball). "When does it finish?" "When it finishes." "Where's the clock?" "There is no clock." Timo looks for the clock for nine innings.

Held back on purpose: a "they moved the match" sketch (the change alert is a paid add-on and needs careful wording) and anything with a casino (the fact sheet keeps casinos out of mascot films until the founder decides).
create:duo.where_the_brand_sits:
In the last three seconds, and in one spoken word before that.

- The fixed ending: Luna says "One sentence, Timo." As she says it, a small card sign pops up between them: the round V crest, VENUVOY, and under it "One sentence. Your sports trip, planned." Three whistle blasts. About 2.5 to 3 seconds. The sign is the only text on screen at that moment. The line and the sign-off wording are the ones the fact sheet already settled on.
- Before that the name is never said and no logo is shown. At most, one of them says "the plan" once ("It's in the plan." "The plan had the official one. First link.").
- The scarf and the paper world carry the brand's colours all the way through, with no logo.
- No card with ticks. No typed sentence on screen. No feature list. No season or episode numbers.

TRUTH, checked against the fact sheet
- "One sentence" is shorthand. In the product the sentence fills in the planner and you then press "Create plans". The earlier films used the same shorthand and the fact sheet accepts it. The post text under each video should say it exactly: "Type your trip in one sentence, Venuvoy fills in the planner, you press Create plans. Planning is free. We never sell tickets."
- Only "plans" and "the plan". Never book, buy, sell, reserve, "AI", "anywhere in the world".
- Tickets: the films never suggest the product supplies, holds or guarantees a ticket. In episode 3 Luna bought the tickets herself from the official seller; the plan only put that link first. That claim is in the fact sheet ("puts the official seller first"). The film must not say "protects you from scams".
- Episode 1 rests on "plans sports trips around real fixtures". It must not say "verified" or "confirmed"; most fixtures are marked provisional.
- Episode 2 says tennis today and baseball tomorrow in one trip. The catalog lists the US Open tennis and New York baseball. Before any still is drawn, check that one week holds both. If it does not, change the second sport to one that is there.
- No flights, no hotels, no bars, no club, league or stadium names.
- Golf rounds and stadium tours only in England; runs and hikes only in the listed countries. The ideas list marks these.

scripts.title: Away (football)
scripts.script:
PLACE: one stand of an empty football ground on a grey afternoon. Rows of empty green flip-seats, cream steps, one floodlight. Timo on the left, Luna on the right, both in the green-and-cream scarf. Timo holds a small paper flag. Luna holds a paper cup of tea.
TEXT ON SCREEN: every spoken line, word for word, one at a time, on a paper strip beside the speaker. Nothing else until the sign.

SHOT 1, WIDE, 0.0 to 2.6 s.
The page pops up in four frames: hundreds of empty seats, two tiny figures in the middle. Timo is on his feet. Sound: wind. He claps the terrace rhythm alone: clap clap, clap-clap-clap. The echo claps back.
TIMO (shouting): COME ON!
(The echo: ...on ...on.)
FIRST-SECOND HOOK: two people in an empty stadium, and the sound of one man clapping.

SHOT 2, TWO-SHOT, chest up, behind the seat-backs. This shot runs to the end.
2.6 s. Timo lowers his arms.
TIMO: Bit quiet.
LUNA (looking at her tea): It's empty.
TIMO: It's EARLY. This is what early looks like.
6.3 s. A small engine starts. A paper groundsman on a ride-on mower slides across behind them, left to right. Timo's eyes follow it. Luna takes out her phone.
TIMO (watching the mower): ...Warm-up.
LUNA (reading her phone): It's an away game.
TIMO: Away where?
LUNA: ...Where we live.
TIMO: Where we...
LUNA (over him): Ten minutes from your couch.
12.7 s. Nobody moves. Wind. The flag in Timo's hand droops on its pin.
TIMO: So all those people in our scarf, at the airport...
LUNA: Were arriving.
TIMO (small): ...I high-fived them.
PUNCHLINE: I high-fived them.
Hold half a second. Nothing moves.
18.1 s.
LUNA: One sentence, Timo.
As she says it the sign pops up between them: cream card, green letters, the round V crest, VENUVOY, and under it: One sentence. Your sports trip, planned. It is the only text on screen.
19.3 s. The full-time whistle, three blasts. Timo's head flips to face us. He looks at the camera. The mower comes back the other way.
LAST IMAGE: the two of them alone in the empty stand, the sign between them, Timo looking at us.
21.0 s. Cut.

TRUE BECAUSE: the product builds a trip around real published fixtures for the place and dates you give. Nothing is said about tickets, flights or hotels. No club, league or city is named.

scripts.title: Quiet, Please (tennis)
scripts.script:
PLACE: the front row of a tennis stand at noon, white and green, hard sun. Behind them three rows of paper spectators in sun hats, heads on pins, all facing right towards the server. Timo on the left: scarf, two stripes of face paint, an air horn. Luna on the right with a paper fan.
TEXT ON SCREEN: spoken lines only, one at a time. The horn and the shush get a sound caption. The umpire's line sits in the middle, in plain ink. Nothing else until the sign.

SHOT 1, TWO-SHOT WITH THE CROWD. One shot for the whole film.
0.0 s. The page pops up in silence. Sound: a ball bounced before a serve. Tok. Tok. Timo's arm rises with the horn.
0.7 s. HOOOONK. On the honk every paper head in the crowd flips to face Timo in one frame. Luna's fan stops.
FIRST-SECOND HOOK: an air horn in a silent tennis crowd, and forty paper heads snapping round.
2.0 s.
UMPIRE (unseen, calm, through a speaker): Quiet, please.
The heads flip back to the court.
TIMO (loud whisper): What? I'm supporting!
LUNA (whisper): It's tennis.
TIMO (whisper): Why are we even AT tennis?
LUNA: It's in the plan.
TIMO: Who put tennis in the plan?!
LUNA: Me. Tennis today. Baseball tomorrow.
TIMO: ...Is baseball loud?
LUNA: Very.
12.6 s. Timo is on his feet, arms up, full voice.
TIMO: YEEEES!
Every head flips to him again. Off screen a ball thuds into the net and a player groans.
UMPIRE: Quiet, please.
(A beat.)
UMPIRE: Especially you.
PUNCHLINE: Especially you.
Timo sinks back into his seat, slowly. The heads flip back.
TIMO (tiny whisper, tiny fist): ...yes.
TIMO (whisper): Wait. Both? One trip?
19.0 s.
LUNA (whisper): One sentence, Timo.
The sign pops up between them: the V crest, VENUVOY, One sentence. Your sports trip, planned.
20.0 s. The full-time whistle, three blasts. Every paper head flips towards the whistle.
THE CROWD: SHHHH!
Timo looks at us.
LAST IMAGE: forty paper heads shushing the sign, Luna fanning herself, Timo looking at the camera.
22.0 s. Cut.

TRUE BECAUSE: one plan can hold more than one sport, day by day, and the sentence can name them. CHECK BEFORE ANY STILL IS DRAWN: that the catalog has one week with a tennis event and baseball in the same city (the US Open and New York are both listed). If not, change the second sport to one that is there. No tournament, player or city is named.

scripts.title: First Link (basketball)
scripts.script:
PLACE: night, the doors of an indoor arena, warm light inside. Paper fans with foam fingers file past in the background. In front: a ticket scanner post with a round light, and a waist-high gate arm on a pin. Timo on the left holds his phone to the scanner. Luna on the right, hands in pockets.
TEXT ON SCREEN: spoken lines only, one at a time, plus a sound caption for the buzzer. The scanner shows a red cross or a green tick, never words. Nothing else until the sign.

SHOT 1, CLOSE on the scanner and Timo's phone, 0.0 to 1.4 s.
The page pops up. BONK. Red light. BONK. BONK-BONK-BONK. The post shakes each time.
FIRST-SECOND HOOK: the red light and the buzzer every fan dreads, five times before anyone speaks.

SHOT 2, TWO-SHOT at the gate. This shot runs to the end.
TIMO: It's just thinking.
LUNA: It's red.
TIMO: Red IS thinking.
LUNA: Where'd you buy that?
TIMO: A guy. Very professional. Big Dave.
LUNA: Big Dave.
TIMO: 'Big Dave's Real Tickets.' It says REAL. It's in the name!
LUNA: The plan had the official one. First link.
TIMO: Nobody clicks the first link! The first link's always a scam!
15.4 s. Luna takes out her phone and taps the scanner. DING. Green tick. The gate arm swings up. She goes through.
LUNA (going in): I'll text you the score.
Timo taps his phone again. BONK. Red.
TIMO (small): ...Still thinking.
PUNCHLINE: the DING after 'always a scam', then 'Still thinking.'
19.6 s.
LUNA (from the other side of the gate): One sentence, Timo.
The sign pops up on her side: the V crest, VENUVOY, One sentence. Your sports trip, planned.
20.6 s. The full-time whistle, three blasts. Under it Luna reaches back and taps the scanner once more. DING. Green. The gate arm swings up for Timo. She had two all along.
Timo looks at the green light. Then at us.
LAST IMAGE: the gate open, Luna waiting inside with the sign, Timo outside looking at the camera, the crowd still filing past.
23.0 s. Cut.

TRUE BECAUSE: for games in a plan the product shows how to get tickets and puts the official seller first. It does not sell tickets. Luna bought both tickets herself from that seller. The film must not say or show that the product protects anyone from scams or guarantees a ticket. No league, team or arena is named. 'Big Dave' is invented; check the name is not a real seller before use.

create:duo.recipe:
ORDER OF WORK, cheapest thing first
1. The script is agreed in words, with its cost. Nothing is drawn before that.
2. Voices are recorded (or generated) and one take is chosen. The take is cut to length. From here on the film's timing is fixed.
3. Stills. The two characters are made once as a kit of paper pieces (about 16 stills in all, redraws included) and reused for ever. Each new episode needs about 8 new stills: the set in four or five layers, the crowd, props, a costume detail. Up to 4 redraws, only for a named defect (wrong shape, stray writing, a piece that does not match the kit), at most two rounds. A still costs 0.022.
4. Animation happens in the edit, not in a video model: jaws driven by the loudness of the voice, pose keys, card flips, pop-ups, shadows, all at twelve poses a second.
5. Video model: none by default. One Veo 3.1 lite clip (0.30, 720p) is allowed per episode only if the paper animatic shows a shot that paper moves cannot do. One take. If it fails once, the shot becomes a paper move. I expect to buy none.
6. Checks before anything is shown: a frame at every caption change, jaw against the waveform, a word-for-word read-back, each claim against the fact sheet, one cold viewer retelling it with the sound off, and the cost report.

SHOTS: two or three set-ups per episode. A hook shot of one to three seconds, then one master two-shot for about 80 per cent of the film, which also holds the sign-off. Episode 2 is a single set-up.
TAKES: voices, eight run-throughs, free. Stills, one take plus named-defect redraws. Video, none.
RESOLUTION: the stills are large, so the film is native 1080 by 1920. Nothing is upscaled.

COST PER EPISODE
12 stills 0.26, voices 0 to 0.15, sounds 0 to 0.10. Typical 0.4 to 0.7. With the one optional clip, about 0.8. Written ceiling 1.50, checked before every paid call. The kit, the sign and the sting are made once, under 1 dollar in all.
Fixes are free: a wrong beat is a moved keyframe and a new render, not a reshoot.

WHAT IS NOT BUILT YET
The edit tool at /home/user/NEXOR-PADEL/venuvoy-ads/src/film/cut.py has no cut-out layer (pieces with pivots, keys, a jaw that follows the audio, shadows, stepped frames). It must be written and tested once. That costs working time, not credits. The founder has also complained about wasted usage, so this must be said before starting.

create:duo.first_test_under_3_usd:
EIGHT SECONDS OF "AWAY": from "Bit quiet." to "Ten minutes from your couch." Ceiling 1.50 dollars. Stop at the first failure.

1. Three style frames of that one moment, 0.07: (a) cut paper with brass pins, (b) flat felt applique, (c) sewn hand puppets. Pass rule, written now: with no words you can tell which one is sure and which one is dry; it looks like a real material with small flaws; nothing is glossy.
2. The kit for the winner: about 14 stills with one redraw round, 0.31.
3. Voices: two people record the eight seconds on a phone, eight run-throughs, free. Beside it, five readings from the dialogue model, about 0.05, so the fallback is known.
4. Build the cut-out layer and render the eight seconds. No credits.
5. One control, 0.30: the same two-shot still as a single Veo 3.1 lite clip, re-timed to twelve frames a second. This shows, with evidence, whether generated motion is ever worth buying for this look.
Total about 0.75. A second round of stills is allowed inside the 1.50 ceiling.

PASS RULES, written before the test
- The characters are identical in every frame.
- The jaw opens on the syllables, checked against the waveform.
- No stray writing anywhere.
- With the sound off, a stranger can say what happened.
- Three people who are not told how it was made are asked "how was this made?" Fewer than two say "AI".
- At least two of them smile at "Where we live."

WHO JUDGES. I cannot hear, and the earlier watching model gave unstable scores. So three people must look and listen. They do not have to include the founder. The founder asked to see nothing unfinished, so they are asked only for words: yes or no to the idea, the names, and who will voice it. If the test passes, episode 1 is finished completely and only then shown.
create:duo.risks:
Plainly, worst first.

1. THE ANGLE ITSELF. A brand duo is an advert form. The Israeli duos became loved through years of paid TV time and famous comedians' voices. This account has no followers, no media money and unknown voices. The form alone will not make it travel. The sketches have to work as fan jokes that people send to "the friend who says trust me". If they do not, this is a tidy ad nobody watches.
2. VOICES. Everything rides on two voices with timing. If no two people can be found, the fallback is a speech model, and whispers, shouts and interruptions are where those fail. I cannot hear, so I cannot catch it.
3. IT MAY LOOK TOO MODEST. Cut paper moved in steps is a taste. The founder's references are polished television. They may see simple paper figures and feel "cheap" or "for children". The answer is adult writing and voices, but I cannot promise their eye agrees. The style frames exist to find this out for seven cents.
4. FUNNY IS MY JUDGEMENT. No joke here has met an audience. I think "I high-fived them" and the DING after "always a scam" are real laughs. The tennis one is the most familiar idea of the three.
5. ONE NOTE. Timo wrong, Luna right, every time, can go flat by episode eight, and Luna can turn smug. Rule 8 and the second ticket in episode 3 are there for that. The catchphrase could start to feel like a nag; if so it should skip some films.
6. THE TOOL IS NOT BUILT. The cut-out layer does not exist yet. The first episode will take real working time. If the image model cannot give clean, separate, matching paper pieces, the kit takes more rounds than planned.
7. TRUTH BY SHORTHAND. "One sentence" compresses a step (the sentence fills the planner, you press Create plans). Episode 2 needs a catalog check. Episode 3 sits near "protects you from scams", which must never be said.
8. LOOKS LIKE OTHER THINGS. Paper cut-outs recall a famous adult cartoon; a pop-up world recalls a famous video game; a mishap signed by a brand line recalls a British optician's campaign. The designs and the line must stay clearly our own.
9. THE AI LABEL. The stills are generated. I would switch on the platforms' AI label anyway. It is honest and it may cost some reach.
10. MUSIC. The founder asked for trendy music. This plays dry, with a whistle and a two-second sting. They may miss it.
11. NOT "SMOOTH", and "drawn" is my reading of one Hebrew word.
12. NO PROMISE OF REACH. Nothing guarantees a video catches on. At this cost, eight films can be made for under ten dollars before judging.

They support two points: handmade looks (felt, clay, yarn) are already sold as AI filters, and the dialogue speech model is documented as handling interruptions and audio tags.
