create:native.name: Timo Is Also Here
create:native.logline: Luna films every sports trip on her phone, and Timo, who is also there, thinks it is a documentary about him.
create:native.why_this_is_what_the_founder_means:
I take the founder's words one by one.

"The presenters, the duo and the face" (15 Nov): two fixed characters, both in every shot, the same two every time. One of the campaigns they named is a pair of hand puppets. This is a pair of hand puppets.

"At eye level": they talk to a phone the way two friends on a trip talk to a phone. Short lines. They cut each other off. Nobody presents anything.

"Authentic": every episode is a moment a sports traveller knows. You cannot see anything at a motor race. Someone added a hike to the football weekend. One friend takes credit for the planning. The places look like real stands and real weather, not a sunset street.

"Funny": each script is one situation with a set-up, a turn and a button. All three read as jokes on paper, with no picture. That was the test I used.

"Nice": they are friends. Whoever loses the round gets the last warm line ("He's a great two.").

"Not as if made with AI": felt puppets filmed on a phone. A puppet has a stiff face and a flapping mouth by nature, so the limits of the tool look like puppetry. No glossy toy skin, no golden light, no slow push-ins.

"Speaks to today's audience": it is a vlog, the thing they already watch. A new viewer needs nothing from an earlier film.

"A plot" in their sense: the first line says where we are and what is wrong. Nothing needs a label.

"Too expensive": about 1.5 to 2.7 dollars a film against 47, with a written ceiling of 6.

"Send nothing until it is finished": the first thing they see is a finished Episode 1.

It also uses Veo, which I read as the model they named on 12 Nov. That reading is uncertain.

Where it departs from their words, plainly. On 15 Nov they wrote that the drawn style works better. On 16 Nov they asked for animation that is "clean, smooth". This is puppets on phone video, on purpose a little rough. I chose it because their newest message asks for authentic and not AI-looking, and because a rough phone picture is where this angle is strong. If "drawn" was meant literally, the same three scripts and the same two-faces framing can be made as flat cut-out drawings for about 0.7 dollars. The jokes do not depend on the look.

I did not flatter the angle. Its weak points are in "risks".
create:native.cast:
KEPT, CHANGED OR REPLACED
Kept: the two names, tall Timo and short Luna, teal for him and coral for her, and the fact that Luna is the one who types the sentence. The founder named Timo and Luna as the faces on 15 Nov, and nothing in my scripts needs other names.
Changed: everything else. They are no longer vinyl human figures. They are two felt hand puppets, creatures, not people. New temperaments, new voices, new way of talking.
Dropped: the cat, the yellow suitcase, the folder, the 42 steps, "Done.", the bet, all earlier story.
Open: only the founder can say whether "start over on everything" includes the names. If it does, the scripts work unchanged with two new names.
Why change the pairing: before, she was right and he was wrong in every round, by design, and the jokes needed earlier episodes. Now both are fools in different ways and each film stands alone.

LUNA (short, round, coral felt, a mop of orange yarn, wide-open eyes)
She films. In her head it is her vlog. She is new to every sport and not ashamed of it. She is the capable one in life: she is the one who planned the trip. Her flaw: she acts first. She sees a switch, she flips it.
How she talks: fast, bright, in fragments. She starts before he finishes. She answers every question with the plain truth and no shame ("It was a switch!"). Right after she punctures him she is kind to him.

TIMO (tall, narrow, teal felt, long face, one tuft of black yarn, felt eyelids sewn half shut)
He treats the phone as a film crew. He speaks about sport as an authority and is bluffing about half of it ("That was one of them."). He never admits he does not know. He never laughs. He is loyal and easily hurt.
How he talks: low, slow, complete sentences, a little too formal. He opens with a claim to authority ("People ask me", "As a rule"). When corrected he carries on in the same tone as if nothing was said.

WHAT MAKES THEM FUNNY TOGETHER
He says how things should be. She says how they are. He narrates. She reports. He needs to be the expert. She does not need him to be, and likes him anyway.
House rules: nobody is humiliated. Who wins the round alternates (Episode 1 Luna, Episode 2 Timo, Episode 3 neither). Both faces are in every shot.

One caution about the pairing. "The woman who knows nothing about sport" is a stale type. I avoid it by making Luna the one who gets things done and Timo the one who bluffs. If it still reads badly in the first film, swap who knows the sport. The scripts survive that.
create:native.look:
WHAT YOU SEE
Vertical phone selfie video. Luna holds the phone at arm's length, so her round face is low and close, a little stretched by the wide lens. Timo's long face is behind and above her. Two faces stacked, one low, one high. That framing is the signature and it fills a 9:16 screen.

THE PUPPETS
Hand-made felt puppets of the puppet-show kind. Fleece skin with visible fuzz and pilling. Hand-stitched seams. Ping-pong-ball eyes with black felt pupils of slightly different sizes. Yarn hair. A flat dark-red felt mouth that only opens and shuts. No teeth. Mitten hands. No legs ever in frame. They are a little lopsided on purpose.
Both wear the same scarf: dark green and cream bars, no writing. Those are the brand's colours. The scarf is in every frame.

THE WORLD
Real-looking places in ordinary light: an overcast track, white arena light, a wet hill. Slight hand shake. Phone noise. Everything in focus, as on a phone. Hard jump cuts, as in any vlog.
Other people are far away, soft, or seen from behind. Nothing in the picture can be read: no signs, no scoreboards, no shirts with letters, no club, league or stadium names.

MOVEMENT
They move like puppets. Heads bob. Mouths flap. Bodies bounce from below. A puppet leaves the frame by sinking straight down.

TEXT ON SCREEN
Only the spoken words as one caption line at a time, in one plain style. Then the closing lock-up. Nothing else. No labels.

NEVER
Golden-hour glow. Glossy surfaces. Background blur like a film camera. Slow push-ins. Empty streets. A product card with ticks.

WHY IT READS AS MADE BY HAND
1. A puppet is a hand-made object. The viewer judges the puppet, not the pixels.
2. What a video model does badly (stiff faces, simple mouths, bobbing motion) is what real puppets do. The tool's limits look like puppetry.
3. Phone softness, shake and jump cuts hide small drift between clips. A vlog is expected to jump.
4. No legs and no walking means no strange gait. No readable writing means no garbled letters.
5. The cheapest setting (720p) looks like phone footage. Here that helps.

What I cannot promise. I have not generated one frame. Whether the model gives felt and not a glossy render is the first thing the test checks. The films will still carry the platforms' AI label (see risks). The aim is that it looks like someone cared, not that anyone is fooled.

THE STANDING LOOK TEXT, copied word for word into every picture and clip request
"Vertical phone selfie video, front camera, wide lens, held at arm's length by a small hand puppet. Two hand-made felt puppets, the kind used in a puppet show: fleece skin with visible fuzz and pilling, hand-stitched seams, ping-pong-ball eyes with black felt pupils of slightly different sizes, yarn hair, a flat dark-red felt mouth that only opens and shuts, no teeth, mitten hands, no legs in frame. LUNA: small, round, coral fleece, a mop of orange yarn, wide eyes; she holds the phone, her face low and close. TIMO: tall, narrow, teal fleece, long face, one tuft of black yarn, felt eyelids sewn half shut; behind and above her. Both wear the same scarf with dark green and cream bars, no writing. Real location, ordinary light, slight hand shake, phone noise, everything in focus. They move like puppets: heads bob, mouths flap, bodies bounce. No text, no logos, no subtitles, no music."
create:native.voices_and_sound:
THE TWO VOICES
Luna: bright, quick, a little out of breath, a woman of about 25. Statements sound like good news.
Timo: low, slow, dry, a man of about 30. He sounds as if he is being recorded for history.
Both in neutral international English with contractions. No slang that will not survive a Hebrew dub.
The contrast is extreme on purpose: the low slow one and the high fast one. If a voice shifts a little between clips, the ear still knows who is who.

HOW THE VOICES ARE MADE: FIRST CHOICE
The video model speaks the lines inside the clip. The mouths then match by construction and it costs nothing extra. The same voice description is copied into every request. After each clip the pitch of every line is measured for free. A line that sits outside the character's range is pulled back by a small pitch shift in the edit, also free.
The honest weakness: this does not lock a voice. The same character can sound like a different person in the next clip or the next episode. For two "faces of the brand" that matters.

WHAT I CHECKED TODAY, FOR FREE
I read the service's public list of endpoints. There is no tool there that converts one voice into another. So the neat fix (let the model act, then convert to one fixed voice) is not available at this service. The list does have tools that take a picture plus a sound file and return a talking video (OmniHuman 2.0, Wan 2.2 speech-to-video) and lip-sync tools that take a video plus a sound file. I did not call any of them. Their results on felt puppets are unknown.

SECOND CHOICE, IF THE VOICES DRIFT
Voices first. Either the dialogue model with two fixed voices (five readings of a line cost cents, so the funniest can be picked), or two real people recording on a phone, which is free and is how the founder's reference campaigns were built. Then the picture follows the sound: one talking mouth per clip with the other line spoken from behind the phone, driven by one of the picture-plus-sound tools; or mouth flaps cut in the edit from two stills (open, shut) that follow the loudness of the voice, which is how a real hand puppet talks.

NOBODY IN THIS PIPELINE CAN HEAR
A person must listen once before a film is called good. That is not optional.

SOUND
The place is the soundtrack: crowd murmur, shoe squeaks, wind, engines. One continuous bed per place under the jump cuts, so the cuts do not click.
No music under the talk. Jokes die under music. This is less than the "trendy, fun music" the founder asked for on 15 Nov, and I say so. On TikTok a track from the Commercial Music Library can be added in the app at low volume when posting. Chart songs are not allowed for a brand account.

THE FIXED CLOSING SOUND
A referee's whistle, two short peeps, made once and used in every film. It lands with the lock-up.
Nobody speaks the brand name in these three films. A generated voice may mispronounce it and nobody here could hear the mistake. Once a person has approved one recording of the name, it can be added to the whistle and reused for ever.
create:native.episode_engine:
THE SHAPE, THE SAME EVERY TIME
Second 0 to 2: a felt face too close to the lens, already in the middle of something. One spoken line says where we are and what is wrong.
Second 2 to 12: the bicker. He claims, she reports. Two jump cuts at most.
Second 12 to 18: the turn, one fact that flips who was right, then the button line.
Last 2 seconds: the whistle and the lock-up over the live shot. No freeze, no separate card.

RULES
One place. One sport. Both faces in every shot. 45 to 60 spoken words. Three clips. Nothing that needs an earlier film. The sport changes every episode. The plan is inside the joke about two times in three, and absent the third time. Who wins alternates.

TEN MORE, ONE LINE EACH
1. Tennis, "Whispering Loud". Timo shushes Luna's whispered vlog through a whole rally ("You're whispering loud"), then screams at a line call himself; the umpire says "Quiet, please"; Luna whispers to the lens: "He's whispering loud."
2. Baseball, "Is It Still Going". In the first inning Luna asks when it ends and Timo says "Nobody knows"; three jump cuts later it is dark, she wears two caps and explains the rules wrongly, and he is the one asking when it ends.
3. Football, "Which Ones Are We". Luna celebrates a goal alone in a silent stand; Timo, through his teeth: "That was them"; she turns the cheer into a long yawn.
4. Football, "Don't Move". They score while Luna is mid-bite; Timo forbids her to move for the rest of the match; jump cuts of the hot dog an inch from her mouth; they concede; Timo: "You blinked."
5. Golf, "Still There". Luna whispers TV commentary over Timo's first tee shot; six practice swings, one real one, a long proud look down the fairway; Luna, softly: "And it's still there."
6. Ice hockey, "Found It". Luna cannot see the puck; Timo explains that you watch where it is going to be; it hits the glass an inch from her face; "Found it."
7. Stadium tour, "It's Touching Me". The guide says do not touch the grass; Timo gives a moving speech about what this turf has seen; Luna tilts the phone down and his hand is flat on it; "I'm not touching it. It's touching me."
8. Any sport, "Easy Pace". The planner made three versions of the same trip; at 7 a.m. Timo stands at the door in full kit for "Big Matches" while Luna, in bed, reads hers aloud: "Easy Pace." (True: it builds two or three versions and these are their names.)
9. Any sport, "Instinct". Timo walks them to the ground by instinct while Luna keeps saying the plan has it the other way; jump cut to a field and a cow; Luna: "He can feel it."
10. Tickets, "Timo Knows a Guy". Timo's "guy" sends a ticket link; Luna pastes it into the link checker and reads out "could not verify"; Timo: "That's because he's exclusive." (True: the free checker says whether a site is an official seller, an authorised one, a resale market, or one it could not verify. Never say it protects anyone.)

Limits from the fact sheet that these ideas respect: the golf round and the stadium tour are set in England and name no ground; the tour is not on a match day; no boxing, darts or snooker; no casino scene with the puppets until the founder decides.
create:native.where_the_brand_sits:
IN EVERY FRAME, SILENTLY
The scarf in the brand's dark green and cream. No logo, no writing.

INSIDE THE JOKE, IN TWO FILMS OUT OF THREE
Episode 1: the product is the punchline. Timo claims months of planning. Luna says "I typed one sentence and pressed a button" and recites the sentence. About 5 seconds of talk.
Episode 2: the product is the cause of the trouble. Luna switched on hikes in the planner, and a run. About 4.5 seconds of talk.
Episode 3: nothing. A brand that sells in every film reads as an advert.

THE BUTTON, THE SAME EVERY TIME
The last 2.2 seconds, over the live shot: the whistle and one lock-up, the wordmark VENUVOY with the line "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." under it, cream plate and green letters, in the lower third. That is the sign-off the fact sheet records as decided on 15 Nov. No ticks, no feature list, no episode number, no "follow". The spoken captions are gone before it appears, so there is never more than one text on screen.
The rest of the brand lives in the account handle, the bio link and the post caption.

IS EVERY CLAIM TRUE
"I typed one sentence and pressed a button." True and exact: the sentence fills the planner and the traveller presses "Create plans". It is also funnier than "one sentence" alone.
"New York. Next week. Basketball. Two of us." A place, a time, a sport, who travels. That is the kind of sentence the product reads, and the product plans trips around basketball games.
"There was a switch in the planner. It said 'hikes'." True: hikes and runs are switches in the planner, and the planner places hikes and runs. Only in nine European countries and about 25 cities for hikes, so the film names no place. One thing to check before recording: the exact word on that switch. I did not open the product, as instructed.
"Tomorrow. Eight a.m. Run." The plan is day by day and can place a run. The hour is story.
Nobody says books, buys, tickets, hotel, flight, AI or "anywhere". Nobody is shown getting a ticket from the product. The puppets are simply in their seats.
The films compress the real steps (sentence, planner, "Create plans", two or three versions). The fact sheet already accepts that compression for the sign-off.

scripts.title: I'm the Two
scripts.script:
SPORT: basketball. PLACE: the upper tier of an indoor arena before the game. White arena light. The court is far below and soft. A few distant backs. Nothing readable.
WHO WINS: Luna.
SPOKEN WORDS: 52. CLIPS: 3.
TEXT ON SCREEN: each spoken line as one caption, one at a time; then the lock-up. Nothing else.

THE FIRST SECOND (the hook): Timo has taken the phone. His long teal felt face fills the screen, a little too close and a little tilted, heavy eyelids, arena lights behind. He is already speaking, like a man opening a documentary.

SHOT 1 (0.0 to 5.0)
0.0 TIMO (low, grand, slow, to the lens): "People ask me: Timo. How do you plan a trip like this?"
3.4 Luna rises into the frame from the bottom edge like toast: first the orange yarn, then the eyes, then the mouth, chewing.
3.6 LUNA (flat): "Nobody asks you that."

JUMP CUT

SHOT 2 (5.0 to 11.5). Same seats. Both faces now. He looks only at the lens. She looks at the lens too.
5.0 TIMO (as if she had not spoken): "And I tell them: months. Research. Instinct."
8.0 LUNA (cheerful, to the lens): "I typed one sentence and pressed a button."
10.0 TIMO (same grand tone, not a blink): "A lot of it is instinct."

JUMP CUT

SHOT 3 (11.5 to 19.5). Luna has the phone back. Her round face is low and close. His long face is above her.
11.5 LUNA (reciting, a small nod on each part): "'New York. Next week. Basketball. Two of us.'"
14.5 Silence. Timo looks down at her. Then, slowly, at the lens. His chin goes up.
15.3 TIMO (with full dignity): "I'm the 'two'."   <- THE PUNCHLINE
16.3 LUNA (warm, to the lens, meaning it): "He's a great two."   <- THE BUTTON
17.3 The whistle, two short peeps. The lock-up appears in the lower third over the live shot: VENUVOY, and under it "one sentence. your sports trip, planned."

THE LAST IMAGE (to 19.5): the two felt faces stacked, hers low, his high. He holds his chin up for the camera. She looks up at him, pleased with him.

NOTES FOR THE SHOOT: no prop has to be handled. If the rise from the bottom edge fails, Luna simply leans in from the side. The set-up is his claim, the turn is her plain fact, and he saves himself by claiming the only part of the sentence that is him.

scripts.title: The Switch
scripts.script:
SPORT: a football weekend with a hike in it. PLACE: a windy hill path above a small city. Grey sky, wet grass. Far below in the haze, the small oval of a stadium. No place is named. Nothing readable.
WHO WINS: Timo. Luna is the one at fault.
SPOKEN WORDS: 56. CLIPS: 3.
TEXT ON SCREEN: each spoken line as one caption, one at a time; then the lock-up. Nothing else.

THE FIRST SECOND (the hook): Luna's round face close to the lens, her yarn hair blown flat sideways, out of breath and delighted. Behind her, full length on the path, Timo lies face down in his scarf. A football scarf on a mountain is the picture that stops the thumb.

SHOT 1 (0.0 to 6.5)
0.0 LUNA (shouting over the wind, bright): "Day two of the football trip!"
1.7 TIMO (face in the path, muffled, not moving): "Why is there a mountain in the football trip?"
4.2 LUNA (to the lens, a little less bright): "There was a switch in the planner. It said 'hikes'."

JUMP CUT

SHOT 2 (6.5 to 12.5). Timo is upright now, close behind her shoulder, a blade of grass stuck to his face. He stares at the side of her head. She keeps her eyes on the lens.
6.5 TIMO: "You hate hikes."
7.5 LUNA: "I like the idea of hikes."
9.1 TIMO: "So why did you flip it?"
10.4 LUNA (turning to him, amazed that he has to ask): "It was a switch!"
11.6 They hold. He stares at her. She turns back to the lens.

JUMP CUT

SHOT 3 (12.5 to 20.5). Tighter. Both faces. His eyes are narrow.
12.5 TIMO (slow): "...What else did you flip?"
14.2 Luna leans into the lens and squints. She is reading her screen, so she is reading us.
14.6 LUNA (small voice, reading): "'Tomorrow. Eight a.m. Run.'"   <- THE TURN
16.6 Timo, with no change of expression, sinks straight down out of the bottom of the frame, the way a puppet leaves. Off screen: a soft thud. Wind.   <- THE PUNCHLINE
17.6 LUNA (sunny again, to the lens): "He loves it."   <- THE BUTTON
18.3 The whistle, two short peeps. The lock-up appears in the lower third over the live shot: VENUVOY, and under it "one sentence. your sports trip, planned."

THE LAST IMAGE (to 20.5): Luna alone in the frame, hair flat sideways, smiling at the lens, the hill behind her. From below the frame, one long low groan.

NOTES FOR THE SHOOT: in shot 1 Timo's mouth is in the ground, so his line can be laid in the edit and needs no lips. The thud and the groan are added in the edit. Check the real word on the planner's switch before this is recorded.

scripts.title: We Should Go to One
scripts.script:
SPORT: motorsport. PLACE: the fence at a race track. Catch fence close behind them, a grey grandstand roof, overcast. The cars are only blurs of colour and noise. Nothing readable. The word "Formula" is never said.
WHO WINS: nobody. Both are fools, together.
SPOKEN WORDS: 45. CLIPS: 3. The brand is not in this joke. It appears only as the closing button.
TEXT ON SCREEN: each spoken line as one caption, one at a time; then the lock-up. Nothing else.

THE FIRST SECOND (the hook): an engine screams past. Two felt heads, one low and one high, whip from right to left in perfect time. Luna's hair arrives a beat late.

SHOT 1 (0.0 to 7.0)
0.0 The scream. The two heads whip together.
0.8 LUNA (shouting): "Was that him?"
1.8 TIMO (shouting, certain): "That was one of them."
3.3 LUNA: "Who's winning?"
4.2 TIMO: "You find out when you get home."
6.0 A second scream. The two heads whip again.

JUMP CUT

SHOT 2 (7.0 to 12.5). Same fence. Luna is looking down into the lens now.
7.0 LUNA: "I'm putting it on my phone."
8.4 TIMO (appalled): "We are AT the race."
9.7 LUNA (eyes on the lens): "Yeah, but on here you can see it."   <- THE TURN
11.3 A scream. Only Timo's head whips. Luna does not look up. He looks back, at her, then down at the lens. He starts to bend.

JUMP CUT

SHOT 3 (12.5 to 20.0). He has bent down to her height. Two felt faces side by side, very close, slack, staring straight into the lens as if it were the screen. Behind their heads a blur of colour screams along the fence. Neither turns.
14.0 TIMO (quiet, absorbed): "Oh, this is great."
15.2 Another blur screams past behind them. Neither turns.
16.2 TIMO (eyes on the lens): "We should go to one."   <- THE PUNCHLINE
17.4 Luna nods slowly, eyes on the lens.   <- THE BUTTON, silent
17.8 The whistle, two short peeps. The lock-up appears in the lower third over the live shot: VENUVOY, and under it "one sentence. your sports trip, planned."

THE LAST IMAGE (to 20.0): two felt faces staring at us, watching a race on a phone at the race, while a third blur passes behind their heads unwatched.

NOTES FOR THE SHOOT: the engine sounds are laid in the edit on the frames where the heads whip, so sound follows picture. A phone cannot film them and show the race at once. It is a cheat. Viewers accept the lens as the screen, and the picture of the two staring faces is worth it.

create:native.recipe:
ORDER OF WORK FOR ONE EPISODE

1. Words first. The script is frozen on paper. It must be funny read aloud. Nothing is bought before that.

2. Stills, 0.022 dollars each. Once for the whole series: one sheet of Timo and one of Luna (front, three-quarter, selfie-close), about 0.13 in all. Per episode: three start pictures, one per clip, each showing the exact opening pose in the place, drawn with the sheets attached. A still is redrawn only for a named defect, at most three redraws per episode.

3. Clips. Three image-to-video clips from those start pictures, 9:16, 720p, each 5 to 8 seconds. Model: Veo 3.1 lite (0.30 a clip) if the first test shows it speaks and holds felt; otherwise Veo 3.1 fast (0.60 a clip). Both prices are flat for 4, 6 or 8 seconds, as checked in the craft brief. Each request holds: the standing look text, the two voice descriptions, the lines in order with the speaker named, one physical action, and "no music, no subtitles, no text".
A trap I found in the service's public request fields today: these two endpoints default to 1080p and 8 seconds. 720p must be written into every request, or the clip costs more.

4. One take per shot. No second take "to choose from".

5. Free checks on every clip: a frame every half second; is there a sound track; are the words right (read back by a speech-to-text tool); which mouth moves on which line; the pitch of each line.

6. Retakes. Only for a defect on this list that the edit cannot hide: the wrong puppet or a missing scarf; something morphs; an extra character; a cut inside the clip; wrong words or the wrong mouth speaking; subtitles or writing in the picture; music added by the model. The start picture or the request is changed first. Once per shot. One retake is budgeted per episode, two is the limit. If a shot fails twice, the scene is restructured in the edit: the line is cut, or it is spoken over the other puppet's face. A vlog allows that.

7. Edit. Hard jump cuts. Air between lines trimmed. One sound bed per place under the cuts. Engine, thud and groan sounds laid on the picture. Small pitch correction per character. Captions, one line at a time, timed from the measured speech. The whistle and the lock-up over the last 2.2 live seconds. Upscale to 1080 by 1920 in the edit. A little phone grain. One 9:16 master.

8. Before it is called finished: every caption read back against the script; every claim checked against the fact sheet; one person listens once.

MONEY RULES
A written ceiling of 6 dollars per episode, checked before every paid call. A free price check before each batch. With every delivery, one figure: paid clips on screen (3 of 3 with no retake, 3 of 4 with one).

WHAT I VERIFIED TODAY AND WHAT I DID NOT
Verified, free, from the service's public endpoint list (saved at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/6c5eacab-9362-529e-a035-ffc0b493a7b7/scratchpad/reset/feed/openapi.json): the Veo 3.1 lite and fast image-to-video endpoints exist and take one picture and a text, 9:16, 720p; there is no voice-conversion endpoint; picture-plus-sound endpoints and lip-sync endpoints exist.
Not verified: whether Veo lite returns speech at this service; whether either model keeps two felt puppets steady and gives the right line to the right mouth; any price other than those in the craft brief. I generated nothing and spent nothing. I changed no project file.

The test is Episode 1 itself, made in steps, stopping at the first failure. If every step passes, the result is the finished 19.5-second film, and that is the first thing the founder sees. Hard stop at 3.00 dollars.

Step 0, free. Freeze the Episode 1 script. Write the pass rules below into a file. Free price check for every call. Confirm each request says 720p and 9:16.

Step 1, 0.13. Six stills: the Timo sheet, the Luna sheet, the three start pictures of Episode 1, one spare. Up to three redraws, 0.07.
Pass: they read as felt hand puppets photographed on a phone (fuzz, seams, uneven pupils), not as a 3D render. No writing anywhere. No likeness to any famous puppet. Both faces fit the stacked 9:16 framing.
Fail: stop. Spent at most 0.20.

Pass: the file has speech. The words are right. Timo's mouth moves on Timo's line and Luna's on hers. Both puppets stay the same. Nothing morphs. No subtitles in the picture. It looks like phone video.

Step 4, free. Cut the film: jump cuts, arena sound, captions, whistle, lock-up.

Step 5. One person listens once and answers two questions: do Timo and Luna sound like the same two people in all three shots, and did you laugh. No human will have heard it before that. Say so when it is sent.

Totals: about 1.10 on the lite path, about 2.30 on the fast path, at most 2.90 with one retake.

create:native.risks:
WHERE THE ANGLE ITSELF IS WEAK
1. The real thing beats the copy. A feed-native vlog is strongest when a real person films it at a real game. This is a generated imitation of that. Two real hand puppets and a phone at one real match would be more authentic and cost no credits. What the generated version buys is a new sport and a new place every week.
2. The format may be late. Vlogs "filmed by" a generated creature have been everywhere since 2025. A viewer who knows them may read the selfie framing itself as AI. A puppet duo is a less crowded corner of that, not an empty one.
3. It departs from two things the founder wrote. They asked for a drawn or animated style (15 and 16 Nov) and for "clean, smooth". This is puppets on rough phone video. They may read rough as cheap. The scripts can be made as flat drawings instead for about 0.7 dollars.

VOICES, THE WEAKEST TECHNICAL LINK
4. The video model's voices are not locked. Timo may sound like another man in the next clip or the next episode. The service has no voice-conversion tool; I checked its public list today. The fallback (voices first, picture following the sound) is untested on felt puppets and costs more.
5. Nobody in this pipeline can hear. A wrong voice, a mispronounced word or a dead line reading will pass every check I can run. A person has to listen.
6. Timing is whatever the model performs. With one take per shot I can trim air but I cannot direct a line. A joke can be right on paper and flat on screen.

PICTURE
7. Nothing was generated for this paper. The felt look, two speakers in one clip and the right line from the right mouth are all unproven here. The model may also burn subtitles into the picture or add music.
8. A felt puppet tends to come out looking like a famous one. Every still must be checked for likeness and redrawn if there is any.
9. No real clubs, colours, grounds or readable crowds. Real fan videos live on those details. Ours will be generic by comparison, and crowds have to stay soft or far away.

PLATFORM AND AUDIENCE
10. These films must carry the AI label. TikTok requires it for realistic generated footage and puppets in real-looking places count. Some viewers will dismiss anything with that label. The label is not optional and hiding it risks removal.
11. Three films prove nothing. An account with no followers will probably see low numbers at first whatever the quality. A fair trial is two or three films a week for six to eight weeks. I make no promise about views.
12. Almost no music. That is right for talk comedy and is less than the founder asked for on 15 Nov. Only library or original music is allowed.

CHARACTERS
13. Timo as the man who explains can wear thin or turn mean. Luna as the one who is new to every sport touches a stale type. I guard against both: she is the capable one, he is the bluffer, and who wins alternates. Watch the first reactions.
14. Keeping the names is my guess. The founder may have meant new characters too.

TRUTH
15. The films compress the product's real steps into "one sentence and a button". Hikes and runs exist only in some countries, so no place is named. The exact word on the planner's switch must be checked by someone who opens the product. If a later script shows a change alert, it must be shown as the paid extra it is.

MONEY
16. The cost figure assumes one retake. Two retakes on the dearer model bring an episode to about 3.3 dollars. The ceiling of 6 holds either way. The request fields default to 1080p; if 720p is left out once, that clip costs more.

create:wildcard.name: Rod Trip
create:wildcard.logline: Two table-football men who have played ten thousand matches and never watched one finally go on a sports trip, still stuck on the same steel rod.
create:wildcard.why_this_is_what_the_founder_means:
What matches the founder's own words:
- "The duo and the face of the brand": two fixed characters, opposite temperaments, who bicker like friends through one situation. Same shape as the campaigns they named.
- "Adventures, comic things": two men who never left a pub table meet a turnstile, a golf green, a basketball game. Every stop is an adventure for them and a place a sports traveller knows.
- "International": table football is played in bars everywhere. No joke depends on a language. The mouths are painted and never move, so a Hebrew version is a new sound recording and new captions, with no picture work.
- "At eye level": small, self-mocking, everyday speech. The camera sits ten centimetres off the ground.
- "Authentic, not as if made with AI": the picture is an old hand-painted object in real places, moving in stop-motion steps. No glossy figures, no moving faces, no lip-sync, no people in focus.
- "More than football": two football men seeing basketball, golf, tennis and motor racing for the first time is the engine of the jokes, not a line on a card.
- "Don't waste money", "send nothing until finished": about 1.2 dollars an episode, written and timed on paper first, one take.
- It works for someone who has seen nothing before. No lore, no labels, no episode numbers.

Where it may NOT be what they mean, said plainly:
- On 15 Nov they wrote that the drawn (cartoon) style works better. This is not drawn. It looks like a filmed toy.
- They asked for presenters. They may picture people, as Timo and Luna were. These are two painted figures on a stick.
- It looks like football at first glance, and they asked not to be only football.
This is the furthest of the four angles from what they have seen. I think it is the one most likely to be sent to a friend. I do not claim it is the one they will pick.
create:wildcard.cast:
TIMO (left, teal). The tight one. He is screwed on tight, literally. A defender for thirty years and proud of it. He thinks he knows sport because he has played ten thousand matches. He has never watched one. He talks in short, flat, certain statements and panics in a hiss. His painted smile is calm whatever he feels. His rule: "No spinning."

LUNA (right, coral). The loose one. Her screw is a little loose, literally, so she hangs a few degrees off straight and rattles when she is pleased. Curious, says yes first. She asks the plain question that breaks his theory ("So who's the keeper?"). Dry, quick, amused. She usually gets the last word, and it is usually a question. Her question: "Spin?"

WHAT MAKES THEM FUNNY TOGETHER. One rod. Neither can go, turn or leave without the other. They have stood side by side for thirty years and have never seen each other's face. He holds back, she pulls, both move. That is every trip with a friend. Five fixed facts feed the jokes: one rod; no usable arms, so everything is done by a kick or a spin; smiles that never change; thirty years on one table, so they know no real sport; defenders by instinct.

PEOPLE. Never a face. Shoes, a hand, a shadow, a voice from a loudspeaker.

TIMO AND LUNA: KEPT, CHANGED OR REPLACED? Names kept. The pairing kept (the careful one and the easy one). Everything else replaced: the bodies, the world, the suitcase, the cat, "Done.", the folder, the 42 steps. Why: the founder chose these two as the faces on 15 Nov, and the notes say the pairing was not what failed. The look, the lore and the writing failed. Only the founder can say whether "start over on everything" includes the names. If it does, the figures can be renamed and no joke changes.
create:wildcard.look:
It should look like a phone photo of a real old object, not like a render.

THE PAIR. Two table-football figures about 11 cm tall on a 40 cm chrome steel rod. A ribbed black rubber handle at Timo's end, a black rubber bumper at Luna's end. Old-style shape: round head, body narrowing to one blocky foot, arms moulded flat to the sides. Hand-painted, brush strokes visible, paint chipped at the toes. Timo: teal with a cream stripe, flat black hair, a chip on his nose, a screw head at his chest, dead upright. Luna: coral, a painted coral bob, three paint-fleck freckles, hangs about five degrees off straight. Both have the same small painted smile. It never changes. Scratches and a little rust on the rod.

THE WORLD. Real places seen from 10 cm above the surface: worn green felt, a plastic stadium seat, cut grass, a steel turnstile. Close-up lens look: the pair sharp, everything behind them soft. The light that is there: bar bulbs, floodlights, grey daylight. A little noise. Framing slightly off, like a phone set down on the ground. The sport itself is never sharp. It is blur, shadow and sound.

MOTION. Stop-motion steps, 12 pictures a second. They slide, tip and spin. Nothing else moves. Light jumps a little between pictures.

COLOUR. Teal, coral, steel, green felt. Yellow only for the small cork ball.

TEXT. One caption at a time, plain bold white, one line, placed under whoever is speaking. Nothing else until the sign-off.

WHY IT READS AS HAND-MADE AND NOT AS AI.
- The things people name as AI tells are faces, lips, hands and floating motion. None are on screen. Painted faces do not move. There are no people in focus.
- The figures are rigid. They are moved in the edit from still pictures, so they cannot melt or change between frames.
- Wear, chips, brush strokes and uneven light are in the design.
- Stepped motion looks like someone moved a toy by hand between photos.
- Every word on screen is set in the edit, so no garbled writing.
Honest limit: the stills are still generated. Whether they pass as a photo is not proven. It is the first thing the test checks.
create:wildcard.voices_and_sound:
VOICES. Two real people, recorded on phones in a quiet car or under a blanket, close and dry. Timo: a man, low, flat, exact, never shouting. Luna: a woman, dry, quick, half amused. Light accents are welcome; this is English that travels. No pitch-shifting to make them "small". Because the mouths never move, any take can be swapped after the picture is done, and a Hebrew dub costs nothing in picture.
If no people are available: the dialogue speech model, five readings of every line (cents), and a person picks by ear. Nobody on the assistant's side can hear. This is the one place a human ear is needed.

PERFORMANCE NOTES. They talk over each other's last word. Timo hisses when he panics. In the golf episode both whisper until the kick. Pauses are written into the scripts and must be kept.

WORLD SOUND. This carries the "filmed" feeling: bar murmur, shoes squeaking on a court, a whistle, golf hush with one bird. The sport is heard, not seen.

THE PAIR'S OWN SOUNDS. The rod: a dry whirr. The kick: a hard plastic clack. Luna's loose rattle.

MUSIC. A short dry loop made from table sounds (rod rattle, ball clacks, knocks on wood) with one bass note, about 105 beats a minute. Low or silent under talk, full for the last 2.5 seconds. Original, so no licence problem on any platform. A person must approve it once by ear.

FIXED SIGN-OFF SOUND, every episode, 2.5 seconds. Luna, off screen: "Spin?" Timo: "No spinning." Whirr (they spin anyway). A ball drops into the wooden goal: clonk. "No spinning" is a real rule of the game (search summaries of rule pages: a turn of more than 360 degrees is illegal). I believe Israeli players know the same rule; not verified.
create:wildcard.episode_engine:
THE SHAPE, 15 to 21 seconds.
1. Second 0 to 2. One picture that should not exist: the pair somewhere a table-football rod has no business being, already in trouble. First spoken line inside 1.5 seconds.
2. Seconds 2 to 12. They bicker. Four to eight short lines. Timo has a theory or a rule. Luna asks the plain question.
3. The turn comes from one of the five fixed facts: one rod, no arms, painted smiles, thirty years on a table, defenders by instinct.
4. The button: one last short line, or a move played on faces that cannot change.
5. Last 2.5 seconds: the same sign-off picture and sound every time.
One sport or one trip moment per episode. No episode numbers. No lore needed.

TEN MORE IDEAS.
1. Tennis, "Quiet, Please". They slide left and right with the rally ("Finally. A sport for us."). The rod squeaks. Loudspeaker: "Quiet, please. ...The two on the stick." "That was you." "It's one rod, Timo."
2. Football, "Nobody Touched Him". Their first real match. "Who pushed him?" "Nobody." "Then why's he on the floor?" Timo: "Thirty years. I have never once fallen over."
3. Motor racing, "Fifty-Seven". Every car that passes spins them like a pinwheel. "How many laps?" "Fifty-seven."
4. Ice hockey, "They Can Reach". A fight starts. Timo, moved: "They can reach each other." Thirty years, ten centimetres from the blue forwards, and he never touched one.
5. Baseball, "It's Us". "Nothing's happening." "They're standing in a line, waiting for a ball." "...It's us."
6. The turnstile. The rod is wider than the gate. Clang. They must go in end first. "After you." "There is no 'after you'."
7. Half-time. Fifteen minutes, a queue of giant shoes. No arms. They come back with a hot dog speared on the rod between them. "Now what?" "Now we look at it."
8. The big screen. The arena camera finds them. After thirty years side by side they see their faces for the first time. "Which one's me?" "The good-looking one." "...Which one's me?"
9. Stadium tour. They step onto real grass. "It's soft." "It's alive." "Ours was carpet." (Only at a ground listed in the fact sheet; tours are placed in England only.)
10. The midfield. Back on the table, the five men on the middle rod say "we're in" for the next trip, then cannot agree which way to slide. A group chat is five men on one rod. Our two type the sentence and go.
create:wildcard.where_the_brand_sits:
EVERY EPISODE: the last 2.5 seconds only. A phone lies on the green felt of their table. On its screen, set in the edit in the brand's own look: the VENUVOY wordmark and one line, "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." Under it the fixed sound: "Spin?" "No spinning." whirr, clonk. No ticks, no feature list, no episode number, no second line of small print. The list of sports goes in the post caption and the bio.

ABOUT ONE EPISODE IN FOUR: the product is inside the joke. Episode 1 is the model. For a man with one foot and no arms, every key is a full spin, so one sentence is all he can stand to type. Then he is angry that leaving the table was that easy. The typed sentence and the "Create plans" button are on screen for 1.8 seconds, as part of the gag. Idea 10 (the midfield) is the next one of this kind.

BRAND TIME ON SCREEN: 2.5 of about 19 seconds. In episode 1, 4.3 of 20.5.

TRUTH, checked against venuvoy_facts.md.
- The films say "planned". Never booked, bought, sold or reserved. No flights, no hotels, no tickets, no "AI".
- The typed sentence names a place, a time and a sport: "next week in New York, basketball, me and Luna". The season notes say this exact sentence was checked against the product on 17 Nov. I did not run the product.
- "Create plans" is the product's real button. The real product has one step between the sentence and that button (the sentence fills the planner and you check it). The film skips that step, as the fact sheet says the earlier films did.
- Sports shown are ones with events in the catalogue: basketball, golf to watch, tennis, football, motor racing, ice hockey, baseball. No boxing, darts or snooker. No club, league, tournament or stadium names. No betting words.
- Golf here is a tournament being watched, not a round Venuvoy places.

HONEST COST OF THIS CHOICE: in three episodes out of four the brand is a sign-off after the joke, not the punchline. That is weaker than rule 6 of the brief. I chose it so the jokes stay jokes.

scripts.title: One Sentence
scripts.script:
PLACE. Inside an old pub table-football table. Warm bulb light, worn green felt. A phone lies face up on the pitch under the defenders' rod. Bar murmur far off.

HOOK, 0.0-1.6. Shot 1, from the goal mouth at pitch level. On the first frame the rod is already mid-spin. Two painted figures whip round once (whirr) and the coral one's foot stamps on the phone screen (clack, a key tick). No text.

1.6-7.0. Shot 2, front two-shot, 10 cm off the felt. Timo left, Luna right. Both hang a little crooked and sway. They are dizzy. Phone glow under their chins. Captions under each speaker, one at a time.
LUNA: "Last one. The big button."
TIMO: "I'm going to be sick."
LUNA: "You're smiling."
TIMO: "It's painted on."

7.0-8.8. Shot 3, straight down on the phone. No dialogue, no caption. TEXT ON THE PHONE SCREEN (set in the edit): a box with "next week in New York, basketball, me and Luna" and under it a green button, "Create plans". Whirr, clack: Timo's foot lands on the button.

8.8-15.6. Shot 4, the front two-shot again. They hang still now.
LUNA: "That's it. Trip's planned."
TIMO: "From one sentence?"
LUNA: "Yep."
TIMO: "We've been stuck on this table for thirty years."
LUNA: "Are you angry?"

15.6-18.0. Shot 5, close on Timo's face: the small calm painted smile, the chip on his nose. He trembles by one frame.
TIMO: "Furious."
PUNCHLINE: that word against that smile. Hold one full second.

18.0-20.5. SIGN-OFF. Straight down: the phone on the felt. TEXT ON SCREEN: the VENUVOY wordmark and "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." Nothing else.
LUNA (off): "Spin?"
TIMO (off): "No spinning."
Whirr. Clonk.
LAST IMAGE: the phone on the felt with the wordmark. A small yellow cork ball rolls in and stops against it.

scripts.title: Hands
scripts.script:
PLACE. A basketball arena, front row. They stand on the edge of a folded seat. The game is never seen sharp: a bright wooden blur, tall moving shapes, squeaking shoes, a bouncing ball, a whistle.

HOOK, 0.0-1.5. Shot 1, from behind and below: two table-football figures on a rod, backs to us. Beyond them the blurred court, shapes running. The rod jerks back a centimetre.
TIMO (a hiss): "He's holding it."

1.5-8.6. Shot 2, front two-shot. Court light flickers on their painted faces. Captions under each speaker, one at a time.
LUNA: "With his hands?"
TIMO: "They're ALL using their hands."
(A beat. Shoes squeak.)
LUNA: "So who's the keeper?"
TIMO: "They're all the keeper, Luna."
(A big blurred shape runs past the lens. The wind rocks them back. They settle.)

8.6-14.4. Shot 3, the same shot, a little closer.
LUNA: "And nobody's on a rod."
TIMO: "No."
LUNA: "They just go wherever they want."
(One full second of nothing. A far roar.)
TIMO: "Disgusting."

14.4-16.5. Shot 4, a little wider.
LUNA: "Disgusting."
PUNCHLINE, in the picture: both tip forward ten degrees, together, for a better look. Hold.

16.5-19.0. SIGN-OFF. Straight down: the phone on the green felt. TEXT ON SCREEN: the VENUVOY wordmark and "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." Nothing else.
LUNA (off): "Spin?"
TIMO (off): "No spinning."
Whirr. Clonk.
LAST IMAGE: the phone on the felt with the wordmark, the yellow ball at rest beside it.

scripts.title: Clean Sheet
scripts.script:
PLACE. A putting green at a golf tournament, at grass level. Low sun. Total hush. The crowd is a soft pastel blur. Everyone whispers, so they whisper.

HOOK, 0.0-2.2. Shot 1, from behind the two figures, looking out between them. A soft "tock" on the first frame. A golf ball rolls slowly straight at us across the green. Far behind it: two huge blurred white shoes and a putter.
TIMO (whisper): "Ball."
LUNA (whisper): "I see it."

2.2-6.6. Shot 2, front two-shot at grass level. Just behind their feet: the dark round hole. Captions under each speaker, one at a time.
TIMO (whisper): "What's that behind us?"
LUNA (whisper): "A hole."
TIMO (whisper): "...That's a goal."
LUNA (whisper): "Not today."

6.6-8.0. Shot 3, as shot 1. The ball arrives. Whirr, clack: one full spin, and the ball leaves the frame in three pictures. No text.

8.0-14.5. Shot 4, the front two-shot. Nothing moves. Far away: a small plop of water. One bird. Then a long, low gasp from a few hundred people.
TIMO (full voice, proud): "Thirty years. Never let one in."
(A beat.)
LUNA: "Why's nobody clapping?"
PUNCHLINE: her question, as a large shadow slides over both of them. Their smiles do not change.

14.5-17.0. SIGN-OFF. Straight down: the phone on the green felt. TEXT ON SCREEN: the VENUVOY wordmark and "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." Nothing else.
LUNA (off): "Spin?"
TIMO (off): "No spinning."
Whirr. Clonk.
LAST IMAGE: the phone on the felt with the wordmark, the yellow ball at rest beside it.

create:wildcard.recipe:
ORDER OF WORK. Script agreed in words. Then voices. Then the whole film cut from stills with the final sound. A moving clip is bought only for a shot that the still version shows needs one. One take per shot.

ONE-OFF SET-UP, about 0.8 dollars, used by every episode.
- The pair on a plain background: front, back, from above, close on each face. Four spin positions (upright, feet toward camera, upside down, feet away). About 20 stills at 0.022, plus redraws.
- The sign-off shot and its sound. The music loop.
- A small addition to cut.py so cut-out layers can slide, tip and swap pose at 12 pictures a second. This is not built or tested. It costs no credits.

PER EPISODE.
- 5 to 7 set-ups. For each: one empty background still, with the pair laid over it from the pose set, or one still drawn with the pair in place from the reference pictures. About 12 stills.
- All movement of the pair is made in the edit: slide, tip, a spin from four pose stills with blur, a one-frame tremble. Added by the edit: small camera shake, light jumps between pictures, grain, shadows that pass over them.
- Video model: Veo 3.1 lite, 720p, 0.30 a clip, at most two clips, and never for the pair. Only for background life behind a frozen cut-out (the blurred basketball game) or a prop with no character (the golf ball rolling). A clip of the pair moving is tried once in the test, for comparison only.
- Text on the phone and the captions are set in the edit, never drawn by a model.
- Voices: two people on phones, or five readings per line from the dialogue model.
- Finish at 1080p in the edit. The source stills carry the detail.

SUMS FOR ONE EPISODE: 12 stills 0.26 + 4 redraws 0.09 + 1 clip 0.30 + 1 retake allowed 0.30 + voices 0.15 + sound 0.10 = 1.20. Episode 1 needs no clip, about 0.6.

RULES. A written cap of 3 dollars an episode, under the 6-dollar limit, checked before every paid call. A free price check before each batch. A still is redrawn only for a named defect: wrong figure or colour, an extra limb, stray writing, a changed face. At most two rounds. A clip is retaken once, only after its start still or prompt has changed. A second failure turns the shot into a still. Each delivery reports paid seconds on screen.

AI LABEL. The stills look like photos, so the platforms' AI label is switched on wherever it is required.

THE VERSION WITH NO GENERATION AT ALL. A table-football rod is already a puppet with a handle. A real two-man rod, painted by hand and filmed on a phone at a real ground, needs no model and no label. It needs a person's hands, which I do not have. It is an upgrade the founder can choose, not the plan. I did not check the price of a spare rod.
create:wildcard.first_test_under_3_usd:
One 8-second beat, the "It's painted on" exchange from episode 1. Planned spend about 1.0 dollar, 1.3 with one retake, hard stop at 3.

PASS RULES, written before anything is made.
a. A stranger shown one frame says "a photo of an old toy", not "a render".
b. The same two figures in every still: colours, the chip, the screw, Luna's tilt.
c. No extra limbs, no changed faces, no stray writing.
d. The motion reads as stepped, like stop-motion, not floating.
e. The beat is understood with the sound off.
f. A person who listens says it sounds like two people talking, not reading.

STEPS. Stop at the first failure.
1. Three look frames of one moment (front two-shot on the felt), three wordings: 0.07.
2. From the best one: the four spin positions and the close-up of Timo, 5 stills: 0.11. Redraws allowed, 4 stills: 0.09.
3. The 8-second beat cut from those stills at 12 pictures a second, with captions. No video model: 0.
4. Voices: five readings of the three lines from the dialogue model, about 0.05. If the founder agrees, two people also record the lines on a phone: free.
5. One Veo 3.1 lite clip: the blurred basketball game behind the frozen pair: 0.30.
6. One Veo 3.1 lite clip of the spin itself, to compare with the pose-swap spin: 0.30.
No lip-sync probe. There are no lips.

IF STEP 1 OR 2 FAILS (it looks rendered, or the figures change between stills): one try at a felt-and-wood version of the same pair, 0.07. If that also fails, generated stills are the wrong tool for this idea. Then the honest choices are the real rod on a phone, or another concept.

WHO JUDGES. Rules b to e can be checked on frames. Rule a is better judged by a person. Rule f can only be judged by a person, because nobody on the assistant's side can hear. No film goes to the founder before it is finished. The one thing that needs a human ear is a 10-second sound file. The founder decides who listens.
create:wildcard.risks:
1. It may simply not be what the founder wants. They asked for presenters and wrote that the drawn style works better. This is two toys on a stick that look filmed. Ask before spending.
2. It reads as football at first glance. The jokes are about every other sport, but the thumbnail is a football toy.
3. All the acting is voice. Faces never change. A flat reading kills every script here. Nobody in the pipeline can hear. Real people, or a human ear on the takes, is a condition, not an extra. That touches "send nothing until finished": someone must hear a voice sample first.
4. The look may still read as generated: bokeh too smooth, plastic too clean, paint details changing between stills. Not tested. The first test checks it for about 0.3 dollars.
5. It imitates hand-made work with generated stills. The platforms' AI label applies to photo-like images, so the label will be on. Some viewers may feel tricked by "stop-motion" that is not. A real rod filmed on a phone removes this, but needs a person.
6. The edit tool for moving cut-outs is not built. Until it exists, nothing here can be made the cheap way.
7. It is not new in kind. Table-football figures coming to life was a 2013 animated feature (Metegol, also released as Underdogs and The Unbeatables). Tiny deadpan stop-motion is Marcel the Shell (2010; its makers say it was shot in two days). One search found no talking table-football series on social pages. One search proves little. The figures must stay generic and must not resemble that film.
8. The rod joke can wear thin. I have thirteen situations. I would plan twelve films and then judge.
9. People may remember "the foosball guys" and forget the name. In most episodes the brand is only the sign-off. The fixed card, the fixed sound and the handle help. They guarantee nothing.
10. Product truth. Episode 1 skips the step where the sentence fills the planner. The typed sentence comes from the notes; I did not run the product. Golf is shown as watching only. A stadium-tour episode is allowed only at a ground on the fact sheet.
11. Whether these are funny is my judgement. No audience has seen them. My order of confidence: "Clean Sheet" first, "Hands" second, "One Sentence" third, because "Furious" depends on one perfectly read word.
12. Limits of my checking. Web pages could not be opened; the three outside facts above come from search summaries: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metegol , https://www.aol.com/news/marcel-shell-went-viral-sensation-143004234.html , https://www.libertygames.co.uk/blog/foosball-the-rules/ . Nothing was generated, no paid call was made, no project file was changed.

The strongest picture and the weakest fit.

"It should look like a phone photo of a real old object, not like a render." (Rod Trip). A photo-real generated still is the picture most likely to be called AI. A flat figure pasted over a generated arena will look pasted.
"jaws driven by the loudness of the voice" (duo recipe). A mouth that flaps to volume looks automatic. Place two or three mouth shapes by hand on the stressed words.

"Each place is a card diorama in four or five layers that pops up like a page of a pop-up book." (duo look). Layered paper dioramas are a stock AI image style, and they push the figures small. "Away" opens on "two tiny figures in the middle". On a phone the faces must be big.
"craft googly eyes" on "hand-rolled plasticine with thumbprints" (cones). It can read as a children's craft clip. That is one step from the founder's word for the last film.
"Both cones look down at it" (the plate) and "the sign pops up between them". Characters admiring the logo is the product-card habit. Put the plate over the live shot and let them ignore it.
"Timo looks at us" at the end of every duo film. It is the stare from the old series, carried over. Use it once in a while, not as a rule.
"A phone lies on the green felt of their table" as the sign-off of every Rod Trip film. It is a separate end card that has nothing to do with the joke before it.
punch_ups: Let her cut him off. Now: "So why did you flip it?" / "It was a switch!". Better: TIMO: "So why did you fl-" LUNA: "It was a switch!" Her answer arrives before his question ends. All the lines in this script are neat turns; real friends overlap.
Change the order at the end. After the thud: TIMO (from the ground, muffled): "Flip it back." LUNA (sunny, to the lens): "He loves it." Then the whistle. Her lie hits harder when it answers his plea.

Make "He loves it." the fixed last line of the series, and "She loves it." when Luna is the one suffering. It is something a person says, it is warm, and people can write it under any video. The slogan stays on the end plate only. Nobody speaks it.

Tighten the one product line. Now: "There was a switch in the planner. It said 'hikes'." Better: "The planner had a switch. It said 'hikes'." Before recording, someone must open the product and check the exact word on that switch.

Direct the readings. Luna is innocent, not sassy: "It was a switch!" is only funny if she believes it is a full answer. Timo never raises his voice, even face down. Record at least five readings of the whole sketch, or two real people on a phone. A human picks the take. Do not draw anything before that.

Build it as hand-moved cut-out, not generated video. Keep the vlog framing: her face low and close, his above. His first line needs no mouth, because his face is in the path. His exit is one slide down. Her hair flat sideways is one pose. Nothing in this script needs a video model.

Help the viewer with the sound off. In shot 2 the wind throws Timo's scarf across his face and he lets it stay there while he says "You hate hikes." It is one more thing happening to him, and it keeps the football scarf in the middle of the picture.
Keep the end plate over the live shot for about 2 seconds, with his groan running under the whistle. Luna keeps smiling at the lens. She does not look at the plate.

For the series, give this pair the best jokes from the other three pitches. Luna reads Timo's trip spreadsheet to the phone: "'Four p.m.: fun.' Aw. 'Four fifteen: fun ends.'" That is exactly this Timo.

Same idea for tickets. Timo knows a guy: "'Big Dave's Real Tickets.' It says REAL. It's in the name!" with the red light and "Red IS thinking." Drop the line "One sentence, Timo." and end on "...Still thinking." and the green light she gives him.
Same idea for "romantic weekend" at the racetrack and "There is a beach. It's near the second stadium." Luna planned both. Timo was not told. The winner still changes from film to film.
Do not make "I'm the Two" first. It is the product joke. Make it third, once people have met the pair. Then "I typed one sentence and pressed a button" is Luna puncturing Timo, not a brand talking.
judge:audience.verdict: Make "The Switch" first, and keep its pair: cheerful Luna who flips every switch, slow proud Timo who suffers. Both are fools, which is fresher than loud-wrong man and dry-right woman. Change the wrapper: no model-made felt vlog. Hand-moved cut-out, two faces stacked, voices chosen by a human ear. Change the catchphrase: "He loves it.", with the slogan on the end plate only. Keep the cones' jokes and "First Link" as later episodes for this pair. Drop the foosball photo look, "One sentence, Timo.", the typed-sentence card, and every line that explains a feature. Still missing: no human has read or heard one line. Fix that before spending.

ranking.why: Best result for the least money and the least risk. The two men and the rod are one rigid object, so one cut-out sprite does all the acting: slide, tip, spin. No mouths, no hands, no lip-sync, no video model. The stiffness is the joke ("It's painted on"), so the cheap method looks like a choice. The still model already in /home/user/NEXOR-PADEL/venuvoy-ads/src/film/s2/shoot.py is a reference-edit model, which suits one small object placed in new scenes. WHERE THE TELLS WILL SHOW: photo-like stills can still read as generated (blur that is too smooth, a rod standing free with nothing holding it); small marks (chip, freckles, screw) will drift between stills; a sliding sprite over a photo can look like an animated photo, not stop-motion; with the sound off only the captions say who is speaking. The four generated spin poses will not match each other. Fake the spin in the edit with a vertical squash and blur. COST: the 1.20 claim is honest. I make it 0.5 to 1.3 dollars a film, about 2 for the first one with the one-off kit. The stage that moves pieces is not built: I searched /home/user/NEXOR-PADEL/venuvoy-ads/src/film/cut.py and found no cut-out layer. That costs working time, not credits. TRUTH: in "One Sentence", "From one sentence?" "Yep." says what the fact sheet forbids ("Do not say the sentence alone produces the finished trip"), and the phone screen with a sentence box and "Create plans" in one view is a screen the product does not have (the sentence box leads to "Fill in the planner"; "Create plans" comes after). "Hands" and "Clean Sheet" make no claim. Photo-like stills need the platform AI label. WEAK POINTS: it is not drawn, the faces of the brand become toys, and it looks like football at first glance. Ask the founder in words before spending.

Deliverable and cheap. No video model moves anything, so nothing floats, melts or drifts, and all text is typeset. Two of the three scripts are strong. TRUTH: I read the catalog data only (I did not run the planner). The New York tennis fortnight, 30 Aug to 12 Sep 2027, has 12 New York baseball rows inside it, all marked provisional, so "Tennis today. Baseball tomorrow." has a real week. "Away" makes no claim beyond real fixtures. "First Link" shows a bad ticket failing and the official one working. That is one step from "protects you from scams", which the fact sheet forbids. Keep it out of the post text. WHERE THE TELLS WILL SHOW: layered paper cut-out with soft shadows is a stock image-model look; a jaw that flaps to loudness reads as an e-card unless each beat is timed by hand; fixed eyes mean the faces never react; one locked two-shot for 80 percent of the film is the static staging the last film was faulted for. The image model will not hand over clean matching pieces. Expect 30 to 40 stills for the kit, not 16. COST: 0.7 is a little low. I make it about 1 dollar a film and 2.5 to 3 for the first. The rig (jaws, arms, pop-up layers, a 40-head crowd) is the most code of the three cut-out plans and none of it is built. Voices carry a shout with echo, overlaps and loud whispers, which are the weak spots of a speech model. BIGGEST WEAKNESS, not technical: "Timo wrong, Luna right, one sentence" is the engine of the series the founder has just asked to start over from, and it still ends on Timo's stare at the camera, the old ending.

The safest thing to build and the weakest result. Two still pictures with eyes drawn by the edit cannot drift. WHERE THE TELLS WILL SHOW: the legs. Eight pairs of walking legs as two-pose sprites will slide, and that is where it looks cheap. Vector googly eyes laid over a clay-look still will look pasted on unless they are shaded. The cones have no mouths and cannot move, so all acting is audio. In "Romantic Weekend" the scene is carried by two people who are only legs, so a film needs three to five voices, the most voice risk of the cut-out plans. COST: honest. About 1 dollar a film, about 2 for the first. TRUTH: "It took one sentence!" is the claim the fact sheet says not to make. "Could've been one sentence" over a landing-time mistake overreaches: the traveller types the landing time into the planner by hand, and the product has no flight search. The rest is clean. The cones never use the product, so the brand is only a plate. It drops Timo and Luna, it cannot do the "adventures" the founder asked for, and googly-eyed cones are the likeliest of the four to earn the founder's word "dumb".

Best writing, worst plan. It is the only concept that still buys generated talking video, which is what failed last time. WHERE THE TELLS WILL SHOW: everywhere. Which felt mouth moves on which line. A voice that changes between clips and between episodes. Puppets redrawn in each start still. Luna rising into a shot whose start picture does not contain her. Burned-in subtitles. Likeness to famous felt puppets. I read the saved endpoint list at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/6c5eacab-9362-529e-a035-ffc0b493a7b7/scratchpad/reset/feed/openapi.json. On this service the Veo 3.1 lite and fast image-to-video requests fix the clip at 8 seconds (not "5 to 8"), default to 1080p, and have no audio switch, so speech from lite is unproven. There is no voice-conversion endpoint, and a pitch shift does not repair a different voice. Timing is whatever the model performs: shot 3 of "I'm the Two" needs a recited sentence, a held silence, two lines and a chin lift inside one 8-second take. COST: not honest under the one-take rule. I expect 2 to 3 takes per shot: 2.5 to 3.5 dollars on lite if lite speaks, 4 to 5.5 on fast, close to the 6-dollar ceiling, with the voices still not locked. The retake rule ("second failure, restructure in the edit") means the film is rewritten by the tool. TRUTH: the best of the four. "I typed one sentence and pressed a button" is exact. The hikes switch is real; its label is unchecked. The recited sentence should be checked against the parser. "We Should Go to One" tells viewers the race is better on a phone, the wrong message for a trip planner. Photo-like puppets in real places need the AI label. Keep the scripts, drop the method.

judge:producer.best_single_script: Rod Trip, "Clean Sheet" (golf). Reasons, as the person who has to deliver it. (1) It depends least on voice acting, the one thing nobody in this pipeline can judge: nine short lines, one physical gag, one crowd gasp, and it reads with the sound off. (2) It needs four set-ups, about ten stills and no video model: about 0.5 to 1 dollar, about 2 with the one-off kit. (3) It makes no product claim, so nothing in it can be untrue; golf to watch is in the catalog. (4) The first frame stops a thumb: two table-football men on a putting green with a ball rolling at them. (5) It shows "more than football" with a joke, not a line of text. Its cost: the brand is only the sign-off. Make "Hands" second and a corrected "One Sentence" third, so the product is inside the joke by film three. If the founder says the faces must stay the two characters Timo and Luna with faces that talk, make the duo's "Away" first instead: it is the best script that keeps them, and it uses the same cut-out method. Nothing here is proven. No look frame exists, the cut-out stage is not built, and no voice has been heard.

Rod Trip, Clean Sheet: "Thirty years. Never let one in." (a beat) "Why's nobody clapping?"
Rod Trip, Hands: "So who's the keeper?" "They're all the keeper, Luna."
Rod Trip, Hands: "They just go wherever they want." (one second of nothing) "Disgusting." "Disgusting." and both tip forward for a better look

Rod Trip: the phone screen with "a box with 'next week in New York, basketball, me and Luna' and under it a green button, 'Create plans'". A product card again, and a screen the product does not have.
Rod Trip: cutting away from every punchline to "the phone on the green felt of their table". It leaves the laugh to show a card, and it confuses a film set on a golf green.
Rod Trip: "three paint-fleck freckles", "a chip on his nose", "a screw head at his chest". Small marks drift between stills and look generated. One mark each.
Rod Trip: "Four spin positions (upright, feet toward camera, upside down, feet away)" as generated stills. They will not match. Do the spin in the edit.
Duo: "Wait. Both? One trip?" A feed line planted so the slogan can answer it.

Duo: "Why are we even AT tennis?" "It's in the plan." "Who put tennis in the plan?!" "Me." Exposition dressed as banter. And "...Is baseball loud?" "Very." is filler.
Duo: an air horn at a tennis match. The most second-hand idea in the pack; the writer says so too.
Duo: "visible brass split-pins at the jaw" with "Jaws flap to the real voice". A flapping jaw driven by loudness reads as an e-card, and layered paper with soft shadows is a stock image-model look.
Cones: "It took one sentence!" An advert line in a girlfriend's mouth, and the claim the fact sheet says not to make.
Cones: "Could've been one sentence." as the last words of every film, including over a flight mistake the product cannot fix.
Cones: "Two googly eyes set close together" on traffic cones, plus "a short bouncy loop" of music. Nursery register. This is the likeliest of the four to be called dumb.

Cones: "It's a very romantic racetrack." Not a joke.
Vlog: the method itself, "The video model speaks the lines inside the clip." This is generated talking video, the thing that failed, in the AI-vlog format viewers already know.

Vlog: "Yeah, but on here you can see it." / "We should go to one." Funny, but a sports-trip brand telling people the event is better on a phone.
Vlog: "ping-pong-ball eyes", fleece, yarn hair. A generated felt puppet drifts toward famous ones; the writer flags the likeness risk and it is real.
All four on paper: stepped 12-pictures-a-second motion sold as hand-made. The founder asked for "smooth". Decide this with a look frame, not with an argument.
punch_ups: Clean Sheet, the sign-off: do not cut to the phone on the felt. Hold the last frame, the two of them under the shadow, and lay the wordmark and "one sentence. your sports trip, planned." over it. One fewer set-up, and the laugh stays on screen with the brand.

Clean Sheet, make the fixed sound part of the story. Under the shadow: LUNA: "Spin?" TIMO: "No spinning." A huge shoe lands beside them. TIMO: "...Spin." Whirr, and they roll out of frame like an axle. That also gives the series its rule of travel: the only way they can move is the one thing Timo forbids.
Clean Sheet, shot 2: frame the hole dead centre between their two feet, so "...That's a goal." needs no thought with the sound off.
Clean Sheet, voices: if a speech model is used, write low voices, not whispers. Whispers are the model's weak spot and nobody here can hear the result. Two people on a phone is the safe version.

Every still request must say what the rod rests on, or the image model will draw a table. On the green they stand on their block feet with the rod level at chest height. In the arena the rod lies across two cup holders. Never floating.

One mark per figure: Timo dead upright with the chip, Luna hanging five degrees off straight. Drop the freckles, the screw and the stripe. Make the handle racing green and the bumper brass, so the brand's own colours are in every frame with no logo.
The spin: one upright sprite, squashed vertically through zero and back with motion blur, three or four pictures. Free, and identical every time. Do not buy four pose stills or a video clip of it.

One Sentence, the truth fix that is also a better joke. LUNA: "Last one." TIMO: "You said that one button ago." Show two stamps, on the product's real buttons, "Fill in the planner" then "Create plans". Then TIMO: "From one sentence?" LUNA: "One sentence and two buttons." TIMO: "We've been stuck on this table for thirty years."
Hands, the hook: open on the front two-shot with the court light already flickering on the painted faces and Timo's hiss "He's holding it." The back view of two toys is a weaker first frame.

Take the truest line in the pack for a later Rod Trip film. Timo narrates his own documentary: "People ask me: Timo. How do you plan a trip like this?" LUNA: "Nobody asks you that." ... LUNA: "I typed one sentence and pressed a button." ... TIMO: "I'm the 'two'." LUNA: "He's a great two." Two on one rod makes "the two" land harder.

Before any credit: read "Clean Sheet" and "Hands" aloud to two people. Then three look frames for 7 cents, with the pass rule written first: a stranger says "a photo of an old toy", not "a render". If the frames fail, the same scripts go to a real rod filmed on a phone, or the duo's paper look.
judge:producer.verdict: Make Rod Trip, "Clean Sheet" first: 17 seconds, one rigid sprite, no mouths, no video model, about 1 dollar finished, about 2 with the one-off kit. Change: keep the sign-off on the last frame instead of cutting to a phone; write what the rod rests on into every still; fix "From one sentence?" "Yep." before "One Sentence" is made. Keep the duo's "Away" and "First Link" and the vlog's "I'm the Two" as scripts; they port to the same method. Drop the generated felt-puppet video, the cones, every fixed "one sentence" scold and any drawn product screen. Nothing is finished until a person has heard the voices; nobody in this pipeline can hear.
